I ask leave under standing order 31, seconded toy the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the situation created by the government's arbitrary action in authorizing a drastic increase of rentals.
There is hardly any need for argument with respect to the urgency of this matter. I fancy the statements that have appeared in the press throughout Canada and the discussions that have taken place will indicate only too clearly to this house that nothing this session, perhaps indeed for many sessions, has agitated the people of Canada so much as the drastic announcement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on Friday last.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate

speechtext:
Order. The hon. member has stated his motion. It is moved under standing order 31, which reads:
(1)	Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (standing order 15) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.

The hon. member has stated the matter.

The hon. member handed me a copy of his motion before I took the chair today, so I have the motion before me.
-who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
My difficulty in connection with this motion is that when the house rose on Friday the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), in stating the business for today, said:
On Monday we shall move to go into supply . . .

Under those circumstances, and considering the meaning of

the word "urgency" as being that it is urgent that the matter should be brought before the house as soon as possible, I think this matter is not urgent, since in a comparatively short time the house will have an opportunity to discuss it.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
The house may recall that before this debate was adjourned on Monday last, I invited discussion on whether or not the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was in order. Since then I have had an opportunity of studying this matter further.
It is quite true that wide latitude is traditionally allowed in respect of matters discussed and amendments moved on a motion to go into supply, and that grievances may be ventilated before the granting of supply. (See Journals, House of Commons, volume 66, page 246.)
On the other hand, there are certain well-established exceptions to this proposition. In particular, citation 467 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, makes it clear that an amendment to 45781-95J
Income Tax Deductions the motion to go into supply cannot relate to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means. At the present time there is on the order paper, appearing in the name of the Minister of Finance, a resolution to amend the Income War Tax Act and the Income Tax Act which is to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, and as the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also relates to the Income Tax Act, it would appear to be irregular in view of the aforementioned citation 467. Also, if the amendment is allowed to stand there would be two motions on the order paper on the same subject at the same time.
Notwithstanding what I have said, in view of the fact that such an amendment might be in order after the budget resolutions are disposed of, and also because there has been considerable debate on the proposed amendment, I feel that it would expedite the business of the house if the proposed amendment were entertained and disposed of at this time. In reaching this conclusion, I should like to emphasize that this should by no means be regarded as a precedent to be followed on future occasions.

When we were dealing with this subject last Monday, I moved the adjournment of the debate. At that time I had no intention of resuming the debate today. I moved the adjournment of the debate solely in order to give Your Honour time to consider your ruling. In the meantime I have decided to say a few words on the amendment.
It is almost superfluous for me or anyone else to try to add to the clear statement made by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he proposed the amendment. But if for no other reason than to emphasize certain points that are important in the question at issue, I shall say a few words.
Let me read to the members the amendment which is now before us. It is to be found on page 1292 of Hansard, and reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the government should give consideration to the introduction of legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to make it possible for taxpayers to deduct trade union dues from income before computing the amount of income tax to be paid."
During the years 1945, 1946 and 1947, a member of a trade union was entitled to deduct his trade union dues from his taxable income. I say "entitled" but he was not allowed the deduction because the
1490	HOUSE OF
Income Tax Deductions rulings made by the income tax branch denied him the right the law gave him. In 1948, a Mr, Cooper, of the city of Winnipeg I believe, a trade unionist, appealed the income tax branch ruling to the exchequer court. He won his appeal. The ruling of the court was that a trade unionist was entitled to include trade union dues as a deduction from taxable income.
It is interesting to note that the government's decision to amend the act in order to overcome the court's ruling did not await the court's decision. Mr. Cooper filed his claim with the exchequer court on April 23, 1948, and a resolution to amend the Income War Tax Act was introduced into this house in May, 1948, which took away from a trade unionist the right to deduct his union dues. The amendment was passed by this house and incorporated in the new Income Tax Act.
The practical effect of the change is that doctors and lawyers still have the right to deduct their association fees, while trade unionists and teachers have not that right. This seems to me to be class legislation, class distinction of the grossest sort. I know there is a distinction made in the act as between income from fees and income from salaries, but that does not make the provisions of the act any the less class legislation. I believe that distinction was condemned by the exchequer court in the Bond and Rutherford cases. It was also mentioned in the Cooper case.
The issue that has been raised in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is quite clear. Let me state it again. The Income Tax Act allows deductions of payments to associations if expended for the purpose of earning an income, if the income is earned by fees. The same deductions are not allowed if the income is earned by salary or wages. Under the law as it stood in 1945, 1946 and 1947, I pointed out that trade unionists were denied the benefit of the deductions by departmental ruling. In replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre earlier this session as to the intention of the government to allow trade union dues as a deduction from taxable income, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) gave the following answer, which appears at page 279 of Hansard:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) :
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The judgment of the exchequer court in
the case of Cooper v. the Minister of National Revenue was in respect of the 1945 taxation year. In respect of claims by taxpayers for that year, and for the years 1946 and 1947, which are _ not statute barred, the department will make adjustments in accordance with the exchequer court decision.
{Mr. Maclnnis.]

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that reply is sheer sophistry. No one knows better than the minister that it is more than likely that any claims that might be made by taxpayers for the years mentioned are statute barred. The claims would be statute barred if they were not made within two months of notice of assessment; and I doubt very much whether there are any cases in those two years in which notice of assessment was not received by the taxpayer more than two months ago. Even then a claim would be allowed only if it was made when filing the income tax form and denied by the department.
Trade unionists found that it was useless to put down trade union dues as a deduction from their income tax, and they stopped asking for those deductions because they found that they were not allowed. I think the government should now indicate its willingness to accept the principle in the amendment, and I think the mover should withdraw it. That would enable the government to deal fairly as between persons in the various trades and professions in this country who must belong to an association in order to earn a living. If the ministers concerned do not indicate that they are willing to do that, I suggest that here is a question with regard to which every member in this house who calls himself a Liberal should be prepared to stand up and insist that the Liberal principle of no class distinctions and no discrimination should apply in our income tax laws.

It is not
often, Mr. Speaker, that I agree with the principles expounded by the opposition. In this matter, however, I certainly feel that the Liberal party are making a distinction they should not make when they say that because a person is in the salary or wage bracket he is not entitled to deduct the fees which he pays to his organization. I cannot see any reason for such a distinction. I must say that I agree wholeheartedly with the amendment on this principle.
There certainly is no shortage of members of the legal profession in this house, and on a number of occasions I have heard those gentlemen say that they cannot follow the argument used by the labour union to the effect that their members must belong to an organization before they are entitled to work in their particular trade. I do not know too much about the barristers' organization, but I feel that they have some such organization which calls for the payment of dues before they are allowed to practise in certain provinces. In addition, when they move from one province to another I believe they have to pay additional fees. If that is not a correct statement I should like to be corrected, but I believe it is so.

It has been contended that we are not working under a free system if we must pay dues to an organization in order to work. For some time I have been in the labour movement, and on occasions have disagreed with the closed shop principle

not for the reason put forward by the lawyers, but because I have felt that it might tend to make a bit lackadaisical the leaders of the labour unions, who are responsible for going out and fighting for better conditions. That is my point of view on that particular question.
I certainly do not hesitate to say, in conformity with what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. _ Maclnnis), that it is a matter of discrimination when we say that because persons are not salaried they are working in a free competitive way and are exempt from this income tax, whereas those who are compelled to pay union dues, or who pay them voluntarily, are not able to deduct them from taxable income. I support the amendment.

I want to say a word or two, Mr. Speaker, in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when the debate was adjourned on October 31. By virtue of the decision just given by you, sir, we have an opportunity to say a word or two upon it today.
This amendment has to do with the deductibility for income tax purposes of dues paid by union men into their respective union organizations. I am interested also in the fees paid by teachers to their professional organization.
At the outset I think I might put the amendment on the record. It appears at page 1292 of Hansard, and reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the government should give consideration to the introduction of legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to make it possible for taxpayers to deduct trade union dues from income before computing the amount of income tax to be paid."
I am drawn into this debate by my desire to correct the impression which I think was given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last Monday night, namely, that the fees paid by teachers into their professional organization were not allowed as a deductible expense for the years 1945, 1946 and 1947, contrary to the position that had been maintained by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
First of all, the facts are as follows. During 1945, 1946 and 1947 at first-and I would have you note the words "at first", Mr. Income Tax Deductions Speaker-doctors and lawyers were allowed deduction of these professional fees-but on their gross income, not on their net income-while teachers were allowed it all across the board. Afterwards, in the Bond and Rutherford decisions, it was agreed that doctors and lawyers were to have that right, even if they were on salary. At that particular point these three groups enjoyed deductibility on income across the board, but it was denied, to men in labour organizations so far as their union dues were concerned.
On page 1288 of Hansard, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is reported as follows:
The act made it clear that people who laid out moneys wholly and necessarily for the purpose of earning an income could deduct those expenses from their taxable income before computing their income tax. The income tax department ruled that in the case of doctors, lawyers and teachers, that provision included the right to deduct their professional fees.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that my colleague has made it clear, as will be seen by the paragraph above the one I have quoted, that he was talking about the years 1945, 1946 and 1947. Let us take a look at the reply of the Minister of Finance:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

In 1945, 1946 and 1947 they were
permitted to do so.
Referring to the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in particular as it pertains to the teaching profession, sir, I should like to direct your attention to the following material. I shall quote from a letter from the Saskatchewan Teachers Federation dated September 23, 1949. This letter was written in reply to a question of mine. The letter read? as follows:
It is quite true that the income tax department withdrew the right or privilege of teachers in Saskatchewan, and I may say in other parts of Canada as well, to deduct for income tax purposes the fees paid to their professional organizations,
Note this:
The first intimation which we had that any change had been made was last spring-
Since this letter was written in September, 1949, the phrase "last spring" refers- to the spring of 1949. I continue:
-when teachers started writing in to us stating that they had been informed that S.T.F. fees were no longer deductible. Perhaps the quotation from a letter received from the Regina income tax office by a teacher in Moose Jaw may make the point clear:
"It is further to be noted for the taxation year 1948 and subsequent years, no allowance can be made with regard to Saskatchewan Teachers Federation fees. Please be advised that Saskatchewan Teachers Federation fees were only allowed as an expense against salaried income with respect to school teachers-"

Income Tax Deductions
And I draw this to the minister's attention:
[DOT][DOT]-with respect to the taxation year 1947 and prior years."
This letter was dated April 14, 1949.
That should dispose of the statement of the minister with regard to these years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was following the court's judgment.

On behalf of the Saskatchewan Teachers Federation, inquiry was then made by the Canadian Teachers Federation of headquarters at Ottawa, and Mr. Croskery in charge of the office applied directly to the deputy minister. He received a letter from the legal division of the department which confirmed the ruling handed out by the Regina office. I quote from the letter received by him:
Prior to 1947, in those provinces where under provincial legislation it was compulsory for the teacher to belong to the provincial federation, the membership fee paid by the taxpayer was considered a deductible expense.
However, in 1948 by legislation enacted by section 3. subsection 1 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948, assented to 30th June and applicable to the 1948 taxation year, a new subsection was added to section 6 of the Income War Tax Act. The new subsection 6 of section 6 of the Income War Tax Act requires that in computing the income from an office or employment, no amount is deductible for a disbursement or expense laid out for the purpose of earning the income. An exception is granted in the case of certain employees of transportation companies, where, subject to the requirements described in the proviso to the subsection, certain relief is extended.
Similarly, under the Income Tax Act, applicable as from the 1st January, 1949, section 5 of this act provides that in the computation of income from an office or employment, no deduction except those specified in the act may be allowed. Membership fees paid to an organization such as the teachers federation and to similar organizations are not among the allowable deductions.
In supporting my hon. friend's amendment, that is the thing to which I object, and which I would ask this government to take into further consideration. That was the new ruling-but note that the date of application is January 1, 1949. As an instance of how government business is done, the letter goes on to say:
We-
"We" means the Saskatchewan Teachers Federation.
We were very much disturbed about it, particularly in view of the fact that we had in our February bulletin advised teachers that the fees were deductible.
That means at the beginning of that year these people did not know that the deductibility which they had enjoyed over the years was to be taken away from them. The letter goes on to say:
It seems to us that we should be given some notices of such changes.

That is the case for the Saskatchewan Teachers Federation.
Another reason I am drawn into this discussion is that the Minister of Finance, in his genial way, and what some of his political enemies sometimes call his flippant way, made some remark about farmers' salaries, just as if farmers as such might not be interested in this particular matter. I propose to quote to him editorial opinion from a well-known weekly newspaper printed in my own city of Saskatoon, which serves almost entirely a farm public. The quotation which I am about to read is taken from the Western Producer of July 7, 1949.
The editorial, which is aimed at bureaucrats, is rather long; I shall not put it all on the record, but I shall take from it as I go along such passages as I consider relevant. I quote:
The activities of the bureaucrats have been exposed many times. The other day there was an interesting example of their methods. It may be worth reviewing here. Mr. Justice Angers of the Exchequer Court of Canada ruled that Joseph A. Cooper, a Winnipeg movie projectionist, was entitled to deduct union dues before making out his income tax for 1945. This case, it should be noted, had been pending for a long time. The decision was based on the parallel provision under which professional men have been allowed to deduct dues paid to their societies.
It was obvious that this ruling would affect thousands and hundreds of thousands who, over a period of years, had accepted the revenue department's ruling that such dues were not deductible. It may be asked:	Why did they accept this in the first
place? The answer is:	How many working men
are in a position to take the matter to the exchequer court? The department, acting as judge in their own case, interpreted the law in their own favour, pretty sure that no one would have the hardihood to challenge their decision. Luckily they were wrong when Mr. Cooper came along as challenger and succeeded.
The judge's decision caused quite a flurry in the Department of National Revenue at Ottawa.
Well it might. The editorial continues- and I would point out that this is the editor's language, not mine:
However, the back-room boys of the revenue department soon recovered their self-assurance. The very next day they came up with the announcement that it was too late for any but a few union members to get refunds from past taxes. They gratuitously admitted that union members would have made savings by deducting their union dues in past years. But as it is, they blandly asserted, the only union members who will now be affected by Justice Angers' ruling are those whose tax cases back to 1945 are still open-a mere handful. The department explained that Canadians are allowed sixty days in which to appeal their assessments. If no appeal is received the case is closed and once closed cannot be reopened. There it is. The moneys wrongfully extracted from workers by the revenue department as a result of its own erroneous interpretation of the law are now safe in the federal treasury and are going to stay there. The public once again has been trimmed and the bureaucrats can breathe a sigh of relief.
A few points may be noted. They say that after sixty days a case cannot be reopened. That is not

true. A case can be reopened years and years afterwards, that is, if the officials can find any loophole whereby more taxes can be levied. True, it is closed against any discovery that the taxpayer has been overassessed as in the cases under review, but not if he is underassessed-a neat loading of dice in favour of the bureaucrats.
Another thing: the department had known for years that this matter of union dues was being disputed. They knew that there was a possibility that judgment would be handed down against them. If they were the servants of the public, as they are presumed to be, surely they should have intimated to this large class in the community that final judgment was still pending, should have kept their cases open and in the outcome, like true civil servants, should have come forward, cheerfully and apologetically with refunds to the people whom they are paid to serve and who pay them for their services.
As a last word:
The important point about all this is not the question actually involved. The important thing is the conduct of the department of revenue. It provides a working example of the new bureaucracy in action. It demonstrates that the men we thought were our servants-civil ones at that-do not themselves so interpret their position. They see themselves as masters-taskmasters-not only of the public but of the legislative and judicial arms of government.
So much for the quotation from that farm paper.
What farm paper is that?
The Western Producer, of July 7, 1949, a weekly paper published in Saskatoon.

I shall wait until the time comes. I do take the matter seriously, and if it is against the rules to quote at such length, I shall not transgress again.
In conclusion, I want to support my colleague's plea for the deductibility of fees paid by union workers and teachers. If we support deductibility in the case of the worker, we cannot very well be opposed to it in the case of someone else. I care not whether a man works with his hands or with his brain; I plead for equality. Either let us permit the deduction of union dues, or let us not have it at all. If it is right that such fees should be deductible for one class, then they should be deductible for all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it might be appropriate if I were to say a word at this point. I shall
Income Tax Deductions preface what I am going to say with the statement that I do not question for one moment the fact that in some cases union dues are necessarily incurred by an employee in order that he may work in a certain plant. It is necessary that a lawyer pay his law society dues in order that he may practise, and for the same reason it is necessary for a physician to belong to a recognized medical society and pay dues thereto. I do not doubt for one moment that it is in the interests of the teaching profession that teachers should belong to recognized associations and pay dues thereto.
Compulsory fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Even if they were voluntary, I should think that the same principle would apply.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out quite fairly that there was a distinction between gross income and net income. As I said the other day, as I have said on numerous occasions in this house and as my predecessor before me has said, the principle of our income tax has always been that salaries and wages are net income. Salaries and wages are supposed to be set at a level sufficient to enable the salary or wage earner to pay such necessary expenses as car fare to and from work, and a number of other things I could cite which are necessary in order that he may carry out his duties.
It has always been permissible for an employer to pay such things as travelling expenses. If a lawyer is on a fee basis, he is entitled to gross his fees and deduct such expenses as rental, stenographic help, bar society fees and the like. If he is on salary his employer is entitled to pay his bar society fees and charge that as an expense of his operations. That happened in my own case. When I started to practise law I received a salary of $75 a month from the firm of which I am now a partner. The partners in the firm paid my bar society fees. When I became a partner, the bar society fees of the juniors were paid by the partners and deducted from the gross legal fees as an expense of doing business. There is no discrimination.
There is a practical difficulty in accepting salaries and wages as being gross rather than net. It has been found in Great Britain and here that it would be practically impossible to administer the act and check deductions from salaries and fees. There are a great many types of deductions besides union fees which could be made. I cited car fare, the cost of transportation to and from work; and there might be the cost of lunches if a worker was unable to get home, the cost of overalls or uniforms in certain types of work. Some

Income Tax Deductions employers do provide uniforms, overalls or tools, and charge them as an expense of doing business.
Those are the practical difficulties in the way. My officials have always believed, and I share that belief, that it would be practically impossible to work out a system of income tax on salaries and wages providing a scale to allow these general deductions from wages and salaries. In other words, it has always been regarded as necessary to consider them as net rather than gross,
Would there be any difficulty in allowing the deduction of union dues?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I should not think so; but if union dues are allowed as a deduction necessarily incurred for the purpose of carrying on business, I do not see how we could stop there. There are many other deductions that could be claimed, such as car fare to and from the place of business, which is perhaps an obvious example. These are the practical difficulties in the way. It is the view which has been taken of the matter in the United Kingdom, in the United States, and here.
There is an alternative practice which is followed in the United States and which we have considered. I am told they allow a blanket deduction of some 10 per cent from salaries or wages to cover such things as union dues, charitable donations, medical expenses and the like. It is a blanket deduction. For reasons which may have been good or bad, we have always resisted that, because we felt that the people who would be most likely to suffer would be the churches and the charities. Human nature being what it is, everyone would take the full 10 per cent deduction, but they might not make the donations which they otherwise would if they could get a tax credit by doing so and producing a receipt.
We have considered the matter, and perhaps it should be adopted. Perhaps it is something to which we will come. It is certainly administratively practical. There would be no difficulty in the department of my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), in seeing that sort of thing was properly administered, because it would be automatic. Another objection to it of course is that people with larger incomes get a greater benefit. Taking it all in all, we have never felt it was a particularly desirable system to introduce in Canada, and that it was better to adhere to the old principle which, as I say, has been followed in the United Kingdom from the time income tax on salaries and wages was instituted, the principle that salaries and wages are net and not gross, and that the salary or wage should be sufficient to


enable the employed person to maintain these necessary things such as the payment of union dues, car fare, and so on.
Do you follow the United Kingdom on everything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, we do not, but our Income Tax Act has been based in part on the practice of the United Kingdom because the principles are similar. We do not tax capital gains in Canada as they do in the United States. They do not tax them in the United Kingdom. Broadly speaking, the structure of our income tax laws has been based on that in the United Kingdom, and I think wisely so. In the United Kingdom income tax was first introduced under Pitt, and we have the benefit of long experience there with good courts to interpret the law. It has always seemed to us that we can usefully benefit from their experience.
I am putting these facts before the house because they are the facts. I have stated them on several occasions. My predecessors have stated them. They are the reasons why, up to the present time, we have felt it was not in the interests of the taxpayers as a whole to allow a general deduction from salaries and wages. There are two exceptions to that rule. I think the hon. member pointed out more than that, but there are two real exceptions. The first is in the case of railway employees. For years that was restricted to railway employees who are on what is known as a mileage basis. Then, for reasons which I need not go into, it was extended to the others. Broadly speaking, it was because it had been done by administrative decision, and once you have given something it is very hard to take it away. It - was looked upon as traditional in the railway business. The railway unions are well organized. They have a scale of expenses established, and I am told it is easy to administrate and is adhered to.
The second exception is in the case of clergymen. That was introduced at the last session.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just a minute. I think the case of clergymen is dealt with in this year's budget resolutions. The other exception the minister has not mentioned is that of salesmen dealing with negotiable contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I announced in the house last year we were going to do this for clergymen. It was introduced in March, and it is again in the budget resolutions. That is the other real exception. There is a third case which might be looked upon as an exception, but in fact is not, the case of the commercial traveller. My hon. friend cited the other day the case of those engaged in negotiating contracts. I have

forgotten the exact phrase, but that is the legal way of referring to the work of commercial travellers.
To put it simply, there is a prohibition in the law preventing an employer giving his employee a fixed per diem travelling allowance. In the case of commercial travellers it was found that just was not practical, and that, although they were on salary and could turn in actual expense accounts, it was extremely difficult and expensive for the employer. The amendment was introduced to enable the employer to pay to the employee a per diem amount for his travelling expenses, and the employer deducted it for income tax purposes.
The hon. member raised the case of private members of parliament who receive a tax-free expense allowance. Again that is an expense allowance paid by the government of Canada for expenses presumably incurred by members of parliament, and unquestionably actually incurred. Those who have been members know that very well. In effect, however, it relieves a member of parliament of the obligation of turning in vouchers to the treasury officers and obtaining repayment of these expenses. I do not consider that as a real exception to the general rule. It is simply an efficient way to enable the employer in each case to pay the actual expenses incurred for him by his employees.
On a number of occasions the government has considered the desirability of making the change requested by the hon. member, and has rejected it. There is no reason why it cannot consider it again, but I believe I should say frankly to the house that my own view, as I am at present advised, is that it is undesirable. I want to point out of course that the terms in which the amendment is drawn make it a motion of want of confidence in the government, and therefore I am bound to oppose it.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the minister's explanation. I wish to say I am still in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I speak in a dual capacity. I am a member of the bar of Newfoundland, and I also happen to be president of a Newfoundland trade union. So far as I can see, the justification for the deduction of trade union dues is just as great as that for the deduction of bar fees. From a practical point of view I see no difference. As to one other comment the minister made, namely, the allowance of 10 per cent that is made in the United States for donations to churches and charities-is that it?
Income Tax Deductions

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Charities, churches, union dues, other incidental expenses of that kind.

Before confederation we had the same principle in Newfoundland except that it only applied to churches and charities. Of course we now come under the dominion income tax rules, and these deductions are not allowable. I believe that is correct. It would appear to me that the suggestion of the minister as to the reason for not allowing the 10 per cent is that he, or possibly the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), does not trust the taxpayer in making his return. We all know what an honourable and respectable gentleman the taxpayer is in making his returns in these matters. I still feel that particular clause should be included. As I said before, I am only speaking briefly, but I entirely agree with the remarks of all hon. members who have supported the amendment. I feel it is one that might very well be agreed to by all hon. members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, the minister just made the observation that he considers the amendment a motion of want of confidence in the government. I am not particular whether or not it is, but I am glad that the discussion has taken place. I believe the minister made the best contribution so far to justify the necessity for the amendment. He stated if union dues were to be taken into consideration for purposes of exemption, then there were a lot of other items that the average trade unionist has to pay in order to maintain his employment and earn his wages or salary. That is absolutely right. Union dues would only mean $3 or $4 a year by way of tax exemption.
This is not a new question to the house. It was discussed in 1940, and I believe every year since then until an adjustment was made. My concern is that there are two most pertinent points that should be corrected. The first is the matter of discrimination. I believe that every hon. member of the house would want to see that removed. I do not think the minister wants to discriminate against anybody. The debate is timely because the budget resolutions must come before the house, and there is opportunity yet for the minister to correct that.
The second point, and I think it is more serious than the first, is the matter of who is working for whom. According to the decision of the exchequer court, for a number of years the income tax laws provided exemption for union dues. However, the income tax people did not understand that decision, or understood too well; in any event they failed to permit the deductions.
No one in this house can say that the interpretation of the law by the income tax

Income Tax Deductions department was correct, and the committee has been shown that the department has wrongfully withheld money which should be returned to the people we are now discussing. I think the time has come in this country when members of this house have to ascertain whether they are working for the civil service or whether the civil service are working for the people of Canada and are responsible to the representatives of the people. There are thousands of very efficient, very decent civil servants in this country, but there are many who take the attitude that this House of Commons and its members are just something to be tolerated for a certain number of months, until they can get us out of here; that we are just a bunch of dumb clucks who have very little understanding of what we are talking about. I think every hon. member realizes that. A great many of the civil servants are very nice, but there are others who have no time to talk to you and do not bother with you.
When the minister comes to his budget resolutions I hope he will tell the house that in accordance with the decision of the exchequer court the government will return this money which has been illegally deducted or withheld from these people. I think he can remove that discrimination; but now that this discussion has focused attention on this matter I would suggest that in addition to deductions for union dues there are other things that should be considered. A commercial traveller gets a car allowance, and all that sort of thing. I am not going all over it again; the minister has done it and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has done it; but I would give the example of the coal miner. Certain deductions are made from his pay every week, money he is obliged to pay. He has to make a payment as insurance that he will have a doctor in the event he becomes ill. He must make a hospital payment, or he cannot work. That mounts up to $52 a year. He has to buy all the materials he uses for blasting his coal underground. That applies to the rock miner also, and it runs into a good deal of money. The miner must pay approximately $4 a week in order to be employed underground in most of the mines in Canada. It seems to me those expenditures are as legitimately a tax deduction as the expenses of the lawyer who maintains an office, a stenographer, and so on. If the lawyer has to maintain his office and spend that money in order to earn a living he is entitled to that deduction; but I also think the trade unionist, the worker who is obliged to make these payments if he is to be employed by the company, is also entitled to a deduction.

That is all I have to say. I think the minister is fair enough to want to see that there is no discrimination as between two classes of people in this country, and that he will take steps to remove that discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the principle followed in the relaxing of rent control.

The minister lives in Montreal, which is a good Catholic city. You know, if you go to confession you are supposed to confess your sins and do penance. I do not know the minister's religion, but there are many good Catholics on that side of the house, and I suggest that they prevail upon the minister to correct what I consider a great injustice and return to these people money which has been wrongfully withheld from them.

Mr. Speaker, I do not feel well enough to speak at length this afternoon, but I do want to express my support for this amendment. I believe it is logical, that it only gives justice to a group of people who are suffering from discrimination. I am not going to repeat the excellent arguments that were put forth by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I listened attentively, and I think they presented on excellent case.
I was also very interested to hear the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) express support for the amendment. In so doing I know he was expressing the views of the organized labour he represents. He has been a trade union leader for a good many years, and I am sure is fully in touch with what working people are thinking about this situation. Personally I cannot understand the discrimination, and that is really what causes me to rise at this time. There would seem to be discrimination against a certain class of people in this country, that is, the wage earner. I do not see why these wage earners, teachers and some professional people should be discriminated against as compared with lawyers, engineers, dentists, doctors, surveyors, architects and others who are permitted to deduct the fees they pay for membership in the organizations to which they are required to belong in order to practise their professions. Why should they be allowed to do that while a larger group of people, earning far less on the average, and whose deductions as a matter of fact are less, are not given the same privilege?
I thought the minister's remarks this afternoon were most interesting, and in many ways I agreed with him. I do not agree with those who say we should allow travelling

expenses, we should allow hospital insurance payments, we should allow this and that. If we started on that course we would have a completely jumbled, unfair and unworkable income tax structure. In this instance, however, I do think the government is perpetuating an injustice involving a large number of working people in Canada in return for pettifogging saving, and I cannot understand why that is being done. In conclusion I would urge the minister to give further consideration to this question, and I trust that later this session there will be some amendment of his budget resolutions.

I am not
going to speak at any length on this question, because the case has been very well presented by other hon. members and it is not necessary to repeat the arguments they have advanced. After having listened to the discussion, however, I am more convinced than ever that there is not a great deal of difference between the fees paid by lawyers or doctors and those dues which must be paid by union workers, teachers and others in that class. The minister mentioned some objections which I think are worthy of consideration, which would make it difficult to frame a workable income tax system in this country. On the other hand, let us consider the lawyer as a professional man. I have nothing against lawyers except the fact that they are one group who are permitted an income tax exemption in this regard. The minister said there were two classes of lawyers, that those who work on a salary were not permitted exemption for income tax purposes as far as their fees are concerned. In order to get over that the firm employing one of these lawyers pays his bar association fees and charges that payment up to the cost of doing business, and I think perhaps that is a proper thing to do. In any event a lawyer does not have to pay income tax on those dues; the firm paid it for him, and he is relieved to that extent. Doctors also are entitled to income tax exemption with respect to their dues. I am not sure whether the minister said the other day that doctors working on salary are not permitted this exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct; they are not allowed the deduction.

The same thing would apply to them. Conditions are entirely different as between these two classes. It is possible for a lawyer or doctor to earn a larger income and thereby take care of his dues. He must pay his union dues in return for the right to belong to that union and work in the particular plant where he
Income Tax Deductions is engaged. I just cannot see why those fees should not be deductible for income tax
purposes.

He went on to point out that, in the case of lawyers who were working for a salary, the employer paid the fee and was permitted to deduct it from his income tax. In the latter case, the lawyer is not only exempt from taxation, but receives exemption from his fees to the society as well.
I doubt if the department would find so much difficulty in administering the act if trade union dues were deductible. The department has an excellent staff which is rather good at tracking down any salaried individual who tries to cheat the department out of a dollar in income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Glad to hear that.

They have an efficient staff which, some way or other, is able to keep track of the salaried people in this country. In the case of Ontario school teachers, their fees to their professional association are deducted by the school boards or by the department of education and paid to those organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why doesn't the school board pay it?
The minister's officials could find out exactly what any teacher in Ontario paid by way of fees to his professional association.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend realizes that the school board could pay those fees?

That holds true in practically all the provinces. In the case of trade unions, practically every local reports to its national office the number of dues-paying members and the amount that those members pay. I am confident that these astute employees of the income tax department could easily check up on any trade unionist who was trying to slip in a dollar more than he actually paid to his union.
I do not believe those are arguments against granting exemptions either to those who pay trade union dues or to the teachers who pay professional fees. These payments are obligatory, just as a lawyer, doctor or any other professional man has to pay dues to his professional organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree; there is no difference of opinion on that.

The minister cannot evade the fact that he and his department are now

perpetrating a discrimination as between professional people on the one hand and industrial workers on the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No such thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, yes.

I should like to say a word in support of this amendment. I was interested to hear the minister's explanation this afternoon. In my judgment he did not make out a very good case for continuing his refusal to allow exemption of these union dues. It is difficult to see the difference between a young lawyer working for a salary for a law firm, and a young union man working for a salary for a company. The young lawyer does not have to pay his fees to the barristers' association because they are paid by the firm and allowed to it as expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The employer could pay the union dues.

I suggest that is drawing the line much too fine. There has been a big increase in the number of Canadians who belong to unions. Unions are of first-rank importance in the national life of this country today. I believe the time has come when these men who belong to unions should be allowed to deduct their union dues. The minister has admitted that there would be no difficulty in calculating those deductions. He tried to tie it up with several other expenses for which claims for exemption might be made but we are dealing today with only one question, and the minister has admitted there would not be any difficulty in arriving at the amount of deduction for union dues.
There is one other feature which I believe is of great importance. The exchequer court of Canada decided this year that, under the section of the act as it stood before, these dues could be deducted. The old section 6 (1) read as follows:
In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(a) disbursements or expenses not wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income ...	.

The exchequer court decided that the last part of the clause entitled members of a union to claim this deduction; in other words, it decided that union dues were "wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income". This case was taken to the court by a union man in 1948; and it is a strange thing-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion that you do now leave the chair permits me to say a word about the report of the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act on Canada's flour milling industry which has been tabled today by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). In my opinion the government cannot escape responsibility for any report that a minister of the government may table. The fact that the minister is required by law to table the report does not in my judgment alter the situation.
Damage to the industry concerned results from the publication of the report and, even if at a late date the courts may later absolve
1500	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act the industry from guilt, the damage is not undone. Therefore, in justice to the industry, I feel that my remarks should be made concurrently with the publication of the report.
I object to the contents of the report only as they apply to the period when the industry was under the control of an administrator of the wartime prices and trade board and the decontrol period immediately thereafter. I have no comment to make about the report of the commissioner on the conduct of the industry prior to that period, or subsequent to that period, since I have no knowledge of the facts.
I do know something about government policy as it related to the control of industries during the war and immediate post-war periods. As Minister of Munitions and Supply I was responsible for the control of a number of industries including timber, steel, coal, non-ferrous metals, rubber, petroleum products and others where supply was essential to the war effort. The control of the flour milling industry was the responsibility of the Minister of Finance through the wartime prices and trade board, but as the pattern of control was the same for all industries I have some knowledge of government policy as it applied during the period in question.
Some months ago the Minister of Justice asked me to look over the report on the flour milling industry prior to its being tabled. I did so and was amazed to find that the flour milling industry was being condemned for carrying out policies that were obviously those of the wartime prices and trade board and those common to all control administrations. To make sure that my impressions were correct I consulted my deputy minister, who was a member of the wartime prices and trade board, and found that my impressions were correct.
Therefore I called the attention of the Minister of Justice to the situation and urged him not to table the report without further investigation and suggested particularly that he consult Mr. Donald Gordon and Mr. Gordon's successor, Mr. K. W. Taylor, for confirmation of the inconsistencies in the report that I had pointed out to him.
The flour milling industry is one of Canada's major export industries. Its sales are made to some fifty-four countries and it furnishes an important outlet for Canada's wheat. It would seem to me a major calamity to Canada if this industry were to be damaged unfairly by action of a government agency. I am also aware that the industry gave the government the fullest co-operation throughout the war years and willingly accepted profit control more onerous than that applied to any other industry.


I was also confronted with the fact that when an industry has been asked to act as a unit in finding a solution of wartime supply problems and in holding down domestic prices, such industries were told that the Combines Investigation Act would not be invoked for acts performed during the period of control. Certain industries asked for this assurance in writing, which was given, but others were content to accept the word of a responsible minister. It was obvious to me that the report under discussion represented a violation of that government undertaking.
Mr. McGregor is, and has been since its inception, a member of the wartime prices and trade board, and responsible with other members of the board for formulating and carrying out price policies. Mr. McGregor was also enforcement officer for all control regulations, including those of the department of munitions and supply. In these two capacities it would seem to me that it would have been his duty to draw the attention of his colleagues on the board to administrative practices which would be objectionable under the combines act. It was a shock to me to discover that, having failed to take objection at the time, he subsequently would attack the industry for its practices during the control period in his other capacity as commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act.
Let us for a moment examine the position of the flour milling industry during the control period. In November, 1941, price control was instituted and prices of most commodities were frozen at their then level. The price of wheat was then about $1.18 per bushel, and the price of flour was consistent therewith. The pi ice of flour was frozen, but the price of wheat was not frozen, and was allowed to continue to find its own level. The flour industry was asked to co-operate with the government to make this possible. Mr. C. H. G. Short was appointed flour administrator, and it was arranged that, if the price of wheat continued to rise, the government would subsidize the milling industry to the extent necessary to assure the industry of standard profits and no more. This meant that the industry must include all profits made from export sales of flour to reduce any subsidy paid by the government on account of losses on domestic sales. In short, the arrangement called for 100 per cent excess profits tax. I might point out that the peak excess profits tax required from other industries never exceeded 80 per cent.
The flour milling industry carried on its wartime operations as directed by the flour administrator. Ceiling prices were maintained on both flour and feed throughout the control period, although the wheat prices

continued to rise. All flour mills were operated to lull capacity and rendered splendid service in meeting the supply problems of Canada and her allies. When decontrol came, the industry accepted direction from the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board in returning to price levels for flour and feed that he considered reasonable. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance said in a public statement that, unless the industry established prices after decontrol that he considered reasonable, controls would be reimposed. It would appear that he was satisfied with the prices then established, although Mr. McGregor condemns the industry for acting as a unit in establishing prices proposed by the board. I would say that both the industry and the government could regard the period of flour control as a perfect example of cooperation between government and industry in the best interests of both the consumer and the public exchequer.
In his report the commissioner states that the industry committed a crime by not selling flour below the ceiling price in competition one unit of the industry with another. I point out that, had the industry done so, it could only have been at the expense of the public purse, since the profits of the industry would have been the same in any event. However, one unit could have dropped its price and enlarged its domestic market at the expense of its competitors had the wartime prices and trade board permitted it to do so, which I am sure they would not. The commissioner also points out the fact that the industry stopped giving away premiums with flour sales. This privilege was denied to all industries by order of the wartime prices and trade board. In other words, many of the actions of the industry complained of by the commissioner were actions directed by the wartime prices and trade board to this industry, and to all other industries.
An important legal action taken against the administration of controls has a bearing on the contention of the commissioner that a subsidized industry should continue to compete unit by unit through selling its product below the ceiling price. This was the case of Joy Oil Company which was carried to the Supreme Court of Canada. The supply situation in gasoline made it necessary to import gasoline at certain times, and where import was necessary the government paid a subsidy to meet the excess cost of such imports over the cost of gasoline supplied by Canadian refineries. The Joy Oil Company imported gasoline and sold it at less than the ceiling price, after which it claimed a subsidy from the government on the loss sustained through selling below its purchase
Combines Investigation Act price. The courts found that the government was not liable for subsidy in those circumstances, and that the gasoline should have been sold at the ceiling price. This would seem to dispose of the commissioner's contention that flour should have been sold below the ceiling price, as the circumstances are completely parallel.
So much for the circumstances of the flour industry within the period of control. Hon. members will note that the selling price of flour was fixed by a government agency, and that all actions of the industry were directed by a government administrator. Mr. McGregor was a member of the team that was responsible for administering price control, being a member of the wartime prices and trade board and its enforcement officer.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) accepted my advice and obtained the opinion of Mr. Donald Gordon which is summarized in Mr. Gordon's memorandum to the Minister of Justice, and which I think I should read at this time for the purpose of the record.
What is the date of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was handed to me today. I am not sure when the Minister of Justice received it.
Is there not a date on it?
No date; the date on the transmitting letter is November 4.
That is 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
