1949. The memorandum reads:
It was impossible during the wartime price control period and the post-war decontrol period to distinguish when discussion and agreements could be regarded as "industry discussions" leading to a combine as defined on page 118 of the commissioner's report or when they formed part of the general wartime supervision and control of a particular industry. For this reason, with the full knowledge of the Minister of Finance and of Mr. McGregor, I gave, as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, orally and in writing, personal and repeated assurances that anything done in furtherance of the substance of the policy and administrative practices of the wartime prices and1 trade board would be held "privileged."
Such assurances were necessary to secure the active and willing co-operation which made the work of the board possible. It should be remembered that exhortation was the order of the day. The winning of the war justified any departure from the normal and, in any event, the public interest was protected by the fact that the wartime prices and trade board was in operation. All this was known to Mr. McGregor, who at his own request acted as enforcement administrator for wartime prices and trade board during the war period. Moreover, I had the advice of legal advisers that the wartime prices and trade board had the legal authority to give such an assurance under the powers granted to the board. In consultation with him on more than one occasion I thought I also had Mr. McGregor's positive agreement that the situation was as I have described. If Mr. McGregor had given me any reason to think otherwise I should

Combines Investigation Act have brought to the attention of the government that a wartime suspension of the Combines Investigation Act was necessary for the price and supply control period, and I have every reason to believe that such action would have been forthcoming. I should perhaps add that in the light of the flexibility of the board's administrative procedures the assurances to which I refer above were not in every case contained in formal documents, nor could they be found always in writing. All concerned, however, realized that there was no difference in principle between oral and written assurances on this particular point.
On the general point, therefore, while I cannot undertake in this summary to debate each and every detail, my view is that the report does not demonstrate improper actions by the flour milling industry during the period to which I make reference and while they were under direction and supervision of the flour administrator and other officials of the board.
2.	Subsidies-The flour milling industry operated at the request of government for a lengthy period on the basis of a drawback or subsidy in respect of flour provided for domestic consumption. This subsidy was for the benefit of domestic consumers and was paid through the millers purely as a matter of administrative convenience. It did not benefit the millers. In fact, the subsidy was operated in such a way as to limit substantially the profits of the millers because of a "profit control" clause in the relative order in council. The special character of this subsidy meant that the full co-operation of the industry was needed to make it workable, and despite many difficulties that was readily forthcoming. It is of special importance to realize in this connection, however, that if sales to the domestic market had been made by the millers below established ceiling prices the amount of the subsidy payable out of public funds could have been increased by many millions of dollars. Consequently, the ceiling price in such circumstances would naturally become the fixed price and, such being the case, any "agreement" in respect of prices would have been meaningless. Indeed, if millers had attempted to make good fellows of themselves by reducing domestic prices habitually at the expense of the public treasury the board would have called them to account. Moreover, under such circumstances of subsidy and profit control there was no agreement in regard to price which could have yielded more profits to the millers unless they had violated price ceilings, and there is, of course, no claim that such was the case.
For the above-mentioned reasons, I am of the opinion that references throughout the report to "agreements" in respect of price during the entire period when subsidies were payable are not only incomplete but misleading unless the effect of the subsidy payment is taken into account. I suggest, therefore, that the reasoning of the commissioner is faulty as it appears in one of the sentences in the first paragraph of page 115, as follows:
"Assuming that in some instances milling companies did choose to sell at less profitable levels,
knowing that they could not retain profits above
a fixed level, the benefit still accrued to the
Canadian public in the form of lower prices."
I repeat that it was certainly not part of government policy that the subsidy be increased through millers offering prices still lower than the already heavily subsidized prices and that the millers were fully justified in preventing this happening. Indeed, I have no doubt whatever that the effect of the subsidy provision was repeatedly called to their attention by the flour administrator.
3.	As already stated, it is not possible for me to attempt comment on all of the voluminous detail provided by the commissioner, particularly since I have not before me the complete documents
fMr. Howe.]
from which so many extracts from context are submitted. Nevertheless, I call attention to a few points in regard to which I am in particular disagreement as to the facts.
Page 22-Uniform Price Ceilings:
The evidence provided here seems to be intended to suggest that improper discussions or agreements took place. The fact is, however, that during the period of price control the flour administrator and" his advisory committee (which included C.N.M.A.) frequently discussed with officers of the board proposals for establishing uniform prices. In fact they were encouraged to do so because the board found the idea of uniform prices attractive as it offered simplicity in a very complex pricing field. The fact that such discussions took place in an effort to reach agreement is not to be adduced as evidence that some sort of a combine was intended. In my opinion the point which should have been pertinent to the commissioner is that, despite the encouragement of the board and despite its willingness to use wartime powers to accomplish this purpose, no practical system of uniform prices was ever discovered and it remained in the realm of wishful thinking throughout the period of control. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that the flour administrator in collaboration with the industry did his utmost to ensure orderly conditions in the industry in the interests of maintaining supply as well as price stability.
Pages 31-35-Agreements on Tenders:
This section of the report brings out evidence as to "agreements" covering tenders, with particular reference to supplies for wartime agencies such as the Department of Munitions and Supply. It should, however, be read with the following in mind.
"Supply" in wartime was often a responsibility rather than a privilege and very often suppliers had to be required to make offers. Therefore, the generalization that there was evidence of an agreement between various sections of this industry in respect to supply and price is not pertinent until it is ascertained whether or not such an agreement was as a result of a procedure required by government controllers. To take the example of ships stores mentioned in this section, my opinion is that the quotations given merely illustrate the plan agreed upon whereby each mill was given in rotation the responsibility of supply. Ships stores were of extreme importance during the war and much organization was required to provide for unexpected demands often made in great secrecy. It was essential that each mill take its turn in the supply line, and this was done with the agreement of all concerned. including not only the industry and the flour administrator, but as well the ships stores administrator and interested departments of government. The ships stores administrator had a great many special arrangements to ensure supplies and exercised wide authority in making sure that no delays were encountered. Not only in regard to flour but, as well, in such things as meat and other food supplies special supply arrangements were worked out and the question of price settled afterwards by mutual agreement. This kind of necessary wartime arrangement must be kept in mind in reading the particular extract quoted on page 35 from a letter by W. L. MacGregor to G. H. Booth, which when properly understood does no more than reveal the agreed wartime procedure.
Furthermore, it also has to be understood that when subsidies were paid the price paid by the Department of Munitions and Supply had a real meaning as to the cost of subsidies-alternatively, if subsidies were not paid the price paid by the department could have easily upset the board's efforts to maintain orderly conditions in respect of price control. It was in explanation of this procedure that the published report of the wartime

prices and trade board covering the period April 1, 1943, to December 31, 1943, makes this comment on page 7:
"An interdepartmental committee on subsidies has been set up to clear problems concerning withholding or repayment of subsidies on goods supplied to the Department of Munitions and Supply and an agreement has been arrived at with the department as to its relation to the price ceiling and repayment of subsidies".
Pages 36 and 63; page 115 (second paragraph) - Decontrol;
The report of the commissioner under this heading does not agree with my understanding of what took place. This is of special importance because I believe the commissioner has stated that his investigation into this industry was commenced because of suspicions aroused by the fact that a uniform price increase took place in the price of mill feeds and flour on the date that price control was removed and subsidies discontinued, namely September 15, 1947. While I was not chairman of the board on that date, I had been responsible for outlining the pattern of decontrol and was closely in touch with the policy during that period. Furthermore, I have checked my recollection of events with Mr. K. W. Taylor, the present chairman of the board.
The situation was that following a long period of price control and subsidy payments everyone was apprehensive about the effect of a sudden release of the controls. Consequently, the flour administrator in collaboration with the chairman of the board reached an understanding with the industry that a flat over-all increase in price be held to an agreed amount when the controls were lifted and until such period as market conditions had settled somewhat and inventories became better balanced. It should be noted particularly that this agreement was at government request and that it dealt specifically with holding the expected increase to a maximum. It is obvious, therefore, that since this arrangement was worked out at the government's request and since it represented a limitation of an increase that would have otherwise taken place, prices would naturally rise to the maximum permitted by this agreement. It is not, however, an agreement of the kind which should excite the commissioner's attention.
On page 114 the following paragraph appears:
"The practice during the war years to which exception is taken in this report is the same practice to which exception is taken with respect to other times, that of agreements to remove competition in price. In the war years regulations established maximum levels beyond which prices could not be increased. In this period concerted efforts were made to prevent competition by securing agreement as to the prices which the members would follow. Such joint action was neither required nor sanctioned by the prices board or any other government agency. Board policy was definitely directed to the maintenance of competitive conditions with respect to prices."
For many reasons the statements made in this paragraph are too dogmatic. As I have already stated, the administration of price control was a highly flexible affair and all sorts of special circumstances had to be met and many qualifications were necessary and justifiable. My previous reference to the effect of subsidy payments and profit control is but an example. There were many other cases in which such things as "production directives", "equitable distribution controls", "allocations for special users", etc., etc., had an influence on price and where agreements were made in order to make them workable. Throughout the period of price control the board strove to maintain price ceilings against the upward thrust of wartime cost increases and severe wartime supply
Combines Investigation Act scarcities. This pressure was so severe that the possibility of selling prices below established ceilings was largely theoretical.
In connection with these and other matters I have not been able to understand why the commissioner did not discuss the facts with me so that I might have informed him of the many interlocking considerations which affected the wartime operations. He apparently did discuss aspects of the report with some officials of the wartime prices and trade board and also examined some board records. However, in view of the fact that during the price ceiling period I was responsible for the over-all co-ordination of all the activities of the board and therefore the person best equipped to inform him, I have been at a loss to understand why he did not invite me to discuss with him these points affecting wartime operations before he completed his report. Had he done so he could have formed a better judgment as to the validity of including any wartime period in his report or, alternatively, have pointed out whether or not the events described during that period were under direction of government officials with special wartime powers.
That is the end of Mr. Gordon's memorandum.
I understand that both Mr. Gordon and his successor as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. K. W. Taylor, expressed their views of the report to Mr. McGregor. Regardless of the views of those who have shared with Mr. McGregor responsibility for directing government policies having to do with price control, the report has now been tabled in its original form.
I claim no special morality, but I regard the carrying out of an undertaking, either oral or written, as a basic responsibility. In this case of the flour milling industry, the undertaking was not given by myself, but I had given the same undertaking to those industries which were under the control of my department. I understand that Donald Gordon had given the undertaking that actions of the flour milling industry during the control period would not be considered violations of the Combines Investigation Act. I am well aware that industries to which I gave that undertaking will consider that, if the undertaking can be violated in this case, it is likely to be violated in their case.
Were this report to be tabled without comment, I would hesitate to again call on industry for the same kind of co-operation that was given freely to the government in working out and administering our system of price control. Incidentally, I consider that governments should have at least as high a standard of morality as individual members of the government, and I know that my colleagues share that view.
Many hon. members will say that Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was not warranted in delaying publication of the report. I do not share that view. After having doubt cast upon the validity of certain conclusions contained in the report by some of his colleagues, of

Combines Investigation Act whom I was one, the report was held from publication with the full authority of the whole cabinet for further checking and consultation. This has now taken place and confirms the objections to the report which were taken when it was presented to the cabinet in the first place. The Minister of Justice took no steps in this matter whatever, except on the fullest disclosure to his colleagues and with full authority of cabinet, which assumes responsibility for the manner in which the report was dealt with.
While the report may damage the public relations of the flour milling industry, that industry can at least know that those, like myself, who shared responsibility for directing its affairs during the control period do not share the views expressed by the commissioner.
I hope hon. members will not draw from my remarks the conclusion that I do not take the view that Canada should have a Combines Investigation Act. On the contrary, I believe that the act is a necessary part of government machinery. Indeed, there is on the order paper at the present time a bill containing amendments which the Minister of Justice is submitting, upon recommendation of the Combines Investigation Act commissioner, to strengthen the enforcement provisions of the act. To be effective the act requires an administration that is both zealous and fair. I am sure that the Minister of Justice will take prompt steps to fill the present vacancies with that thought in mind.
I sincerely hope that those who read the report that has been tabled today will read it with the correspondence tabled by the Minister of Justice, and with the Hansard record of my remarks.

Mr
Speaker, I did not expect this matter to be discussed today. It is a most unusual procedure, on a motion of one minister to go into supply, for another minister to place such a matter as this before the house and thereby prevent the motion being passed. I do not intend to deal at any length with the facts because it is impossible to refer to the evidence and to the findings on the flour milling industry, since the report was just tabled.
There are some circumstances that have not been explained by the minister. I shall read the first section of the Combines Investigation Act under which this report was made. After all, if we are to have in this country a government by laws and not men, then the laws passed by parliament should be observed, and above all by members of the cabinet. Section 27 of the Combines
Investigation Act-it is a rather lengthy section, but I believe it is necessary to have it on the record-reads as follows:
(1)	The commissioner at the conclusion of every investigation which he conducts shall make a report in writing and without delay transmit it to the minister. Such report shall set out fully the conclusions reached, the action, if any, taken, and any other material which may be required by regulation under this act.
(2)	Within thirty days following the transmission of such report to the minister the commissioner shall cause to be delivered into the custody from which they came, if not already so delivered, all books, papers, records and other documents in his possession as evidence relating to the investigation, unless with respect to particular documents the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of any province within which an offence is reported to have been committed certifies that such documents shall be retained by the commissioner for purposes of prosecution.
The next is a subsection dealing with the admissibility in evidence of copies, to which I do not intend to make reference. Subsections 3 and 4 read as follows:
(3)	Every special commissioner at the conclusion of the investigation which he conducts shall make a report in writing which he shall sign and transmit to the commissioner, together with the evidence taken at the investigation, certified by the special commissioner, and all documents and papers relating to the investigation remaining in his custody; and the commissioner shall without delay transmit the report to the minister.
(4)	The minister may call for an interim report at any time, and it shall be the duty of the commissioner or special commissioner, as the case may be, whenever thereunto required by the minister, to render an interim report setting out the action taken, the evidence obtained and any conclusions reached at the date thereof.
(5)	Any report of the commissioner or of a special commissioner,-
This is the particular section to which my attention will be directed.
-other than an interim report or a report of a preliminary inquiry under section thirteen of this act, shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public, unless the commissioner states in writing to the minister that he believes the public interest would be better served by withholding publication, in which case the minister may decide whether the report, either in whole or in part, shall be made public.
Parliament has the right to expect that ministers of the crown shall live up to the provisions of statutes passed by parliament; for if these be not lived up to, parliamentary responsibility ends, and a contempt of parliament occurs which should not be permitted to pass uncensured.
The minister stated that the facts and conclusions in this report were, in his opinion, unjustified. That statement does not answer or justify the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) failing to discharge his obligatory responsibilities under the provisions of an act passed by parliament. Only three years ago in this house I was one of those who stated that in

my opinion-and I know there were some who criticized me for this view-we should alter the provision with regard to publishing these reports in order that no one should be found guilty before the bar of public opinion without having the opportunity of answering in the courts.
The then Minister of Justice answered me and rather ridiculed that viewpoint. Let me ask this question. If this report had been tabled or had been published in February last, what harm would have been done to the milling companies that will not result today? The explanation made by the right hon. gentleman was to all intents and purposes a smokescreen in order to avoid responsibility for failing to perform a mandatory requirement in a statute. Could he not have done the same thing in February when, under law, the Minister of Justice was required-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: January.
In January, if you will. I make it February. Yes, it would be January.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Fifteen days from December 29 would bring it to January 13.

Yes. Would any greater harm have been done then than will be done today? Were there not available to the minister and to the government in the month of January the same answers and the same qualifications that are available now? This action on the part of the government, Mr. Speaker, is the most flagrant disregard of parliament that has ever been exhibited by a government that has never been too careful of parliamentary rules, regulations and proprieties. It is not a question of the guilt or innocence of these companies. There can be only one reason why that report was not published in January. That reason is that an election campaign was in the offing. There is no other.
The government's action in this matter cannot be laughed off. It strikes at the vitals of our democratic system; for if we cannot rely on ministers of the crown or on the government to do those things which, under law, they are required to do, we in the opposition, instead of being able to accept what ministers of the government say and to believe that they are carrying out their responsibilities under the law, are actually placed in a position where we must begin to wonder. I doubt whether we would have had the report yet if the commissioner had not resigned and brought the matter to a head.
I am not entering into the question raised by the right hon. gentleman as to whether or not a monopoly existed within the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. I
Combines Investigation Act am not here to endeavour to try anyone. That is what the courts are for. I am here as a member of parliament to ask why the Minister of Justice, who stands as the embodiment of justice in our land-which means justice under law-has himself failed to carry out a provision that was placed in the law not by the opposition but by parliament. This is an extremely serious matter. I am not going into the record of this government with regard to combines prosecutions. I remember hearing the former prime minister, on election night in 1935, promising that all monopoly privilege would end. Some prosecutions have taken place since then. I think of the tobacco companies prosecution. Those interested in ascertaining what happened and how it happened should read the reports in connection with that prosecution in 1938.
Then there was the dental companies prosecution. That prosecution against eighteen defendants failed because the counsel for the government failed under instructions to prove the signatures on any of the 1,800 documents filed, or that any of the persons were authorized to write these letters. Anyone knows that when a limited company is prosecuted for a criminal offence knowledge must be brought to the directors. They failed to prove that the companies were even incorporated. Mr. Justice Barlow directed the jury to bring in a verdict of not guilty, and the jury acquitted all defendants. I asked the then Minister of Justice whether there had been a mistake in the prosecution and in effect he said that we were trying out this case to ascertain whether or not the combines act would cover such things as we failed to prove. Was it not a strange thing, Mr. Speaker, that they picked the greatest prosecution ever taken in this country to experiment with the law and with the law of evidence?
Champions of the poor man.

That is not all. In 1946 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), then Minister of Justice, made a great speech on the subject of combines and monopoly privilege. He said, in effect, "What we have to do is to put teeth in the law". Mr. Speaker, there are enough teeth in the law; but if the teeth are not used they might just as well be false teeth. Teeth in the law! It was not a lack of teeth in the law that resulted in the outcome so far as the prosecution of the dental companies case was concerned. It is not for me to say that there would have been a verdict of guilty in any case, but at least there would have been a case to call on the defence if the ordinary rules of evidence had been followed.

Combines Investigation Act
I suggest, Mr. Speaker-and I cannot refer to the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act which are to be brought down, though they are merely minor matters-that a law is only as strong as the will of those who act for the crown. A law can be full of teeth, but if the teeth are not used to bite with the law becomes a mere sham on the statute books. Sir, believing, as I always have, that it is not for parliament to deal with the wrongdoings of anyone allegedly condemned in a report, 1 refrain from saying anything about the facts in this matter. I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) whether in the long history of the Canadian parliament, and in the longer history of British parliaments, he can point out a case where in the past any minister has ever failed to discharge the obligatory and mandatory provisions of a statute, unless it be under order in council under emergency legislation in which case the minister appears before parliament and advises parliament that he has taken that stand and stands or falls by what parliament decides.
Sir, I will not labour it, the statute provides what shall be done. Shall there be one in our country above the law? Shall the cabinet be above the law? Is there anyone who will answer me and say yes to my question? If so, we have indeed in this country a government of men, not of laws. I know something of the record of this government. I think of the case taken under law by Mr. Oatway against the wheat board. When he appealed, as was his right under our law, the government passed an order in council to deny him the right to proceed.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, at the time of adjournment I was referring to the Oatway case as an example of arbitrary action on the part of the government against an individual citizen of this country. It would appear that that order in council was passed at the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Another matter to which I might refer is the amendment of the Aeronautics Act with regard to the operation of air lines by railroad companies. That passed parliament over the protests of the opposition and was to the effect that within one year after the end of the war in Europe all railroad companies would have to dissociate themselves from ownership of air lines. A period of a year passed. When asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)


why this statute of parliament was changed or altered, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that it was done under order in council. Later on, finding that there was no order in council, he stated that it was changed under a minute of the cabinet. In those instances that I have placed before you is indicated a cavalier disregard of the rights of parliament and of law as passed by parliament. That is particularly so in so far as the amendment to the Aeronautics Act is concerned.
The minister comes before us and indicates that in a large measure he under the authority of his position was responsible for the nonpublication of this report. I bring to your attention again the wording of the. statute, which is as follows:
Any report of the commissioner . . .
I am reading only the pertinent parts:
. . . shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public, unless the commissioner states in writing to the minister that he believes the public interest would be better served by withholding publication.
There was no authority for doing what the government did in this case and their action constitutes a serious infringement of the rights of parliament. The minister gave as the reason for non-publication that injustice would be done to companies that had operated under certain arrangements between the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board and themselves. Parliament has never heard of those arrangements; parliament has never heard of the terms; parliament is entitled to more than an ex parte statement by the minister of what Mr. Gordon has said in this regard.
Apparently the ministers did not get together on their explanations. I do not blame the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) solely for the failure to publish the report. He was apparently pushed around in this matter. I am sure that he would not have done this as the custodian of justice in this country unless he had been ordered to do so. The Minister of Justice is the fountainhead of justice, and justice cannot be maintained except under law. Justice is not something administered according to the caprice of one cabinet minister or the cabinet as a whole. The minister had a somewhat different explanation the other day when he wrote to Mr. McGregor. In his letter of November 4 he said this:
The government decided not to publish the report or act upon it until the doubts raised had been cleared up. Moreover, in view of these doubts and of substantial increases in the difficulties of prosecuting created by the judgment of the Ontario court of appeals in the dental supplies case, we felt that if we published the report and were challenged to prosecute upon it, we might not be able to make out a case-

How often were they challenged to prosecute in regard to the optical report? As the then minister of justice said in 1946, speaking in this house, the fact that a report is made does not mean that the government has to prosecute. The minister goes on to say in his letter:
-and that such a failure, coming on top of our loss of the dental case, would certainly not enhance the prestige of the combines investigation commission or of the government.
Summarized, the minister's explanation of the reason for his failure to carry out the law was: If we did publish and were challenged to prosecute; if we did prosecute and did not succeed; if there was another debacle as there was in the dental case, it might be hard to explain. The minister goes on:
The government therefore took the responsibility of withholding publication of your report pending the amendment of the Combines Investigation Act to cure the difficulties created by the dental supplies judgment.
That was not the explanation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The explanation of the Minister of Justice on November 4, in his letter to Mr. McGregor, for not going ahead was that the Combines Investigation Act was to be amended and the r eport should not be published until that was done. I give the minister the opportunity to reply to this question: If the Combines Investigation Act is amended to cover the shortcomings of the dental case, does the government intend to prosecute and to use those amendments, which I expect this parliament will pass, in connection with any prosecutions that might be taken as of this date under reports that have been made by the commissioner?
There can be no justification for hiding the report, and hidden it was against the provisions of the statute, a statute that the Minister of Justice is charged with administering and upon whose shoulders is placed a mandatory responsibility. Dare the minister say that statutes of parliament can be suspended by the government because it is not considered judicious to do what a statute says shall be done? Is a time limit in a statute to be made dependent upon the wish or caprice of a minister of the crown?
Surely the Minister of Justice will not stand in his place and say that the government, which for years has on so many occasions shown a tendency to act in this autocratic manner, has arrived at a state of mind where it believes that statutes passed by parliament are to be the playthings of the cabinet just because it is considered to be injudicious to act as the statute demands?
The reason given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was that certain representations were made to the companies by Mr. Combines Investigation Act Gordon. We do not know what they were. We do not know what Mr. Gordon said or what he wrote although that has been asked for by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well). Everything that the minister has stated to have taken place could have been considered by the government in extenuation when it was determining whether or not prosecution should take place. None of the matters that he has raised, no excuse he may offer, can justify the government's departure from its bounden responsibilities under a statute.
During the days of war, by order in council the government amended and suspended statutes. It got the power to do certain things, first under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act and then latterly after the war under the Transitional Measures Act. But even under the Transitional Measures Act there is no longer power vested in the government, or in any minister of the cabinet or in the governor in council, to alter the operation of a statute in any way. I will not read what the minister of justice said in 1946 except to summarize it in this way. The publication of a report is a deterrent and warning.
Tn the optical case grave charges were made against the optical companies. I was one of those who felt, as I said when I began my remarks this afternoon, that possibly parliament should alter this portion of the statute providing for publication of the reports before trial. The law requiring publication was brought in after a Liberal government came into power following the election of 1935. Provision for publication of these reports was introduced by a Liberal government newly in power and inspired in its determination to remove monopoly privilege from this country. Yet the first government to introduce it is now the government that say, when its operation does not suit the wishes of the government, that the statute may be evaded in the manner that suits the government of the day.
I will not say any more on this occasion. More will be said; more must be said. Parliament and the people of Canada have a right to demand that the law be administered equally to all and that no minister or ministers of the government can by their own ipse dixit say that they are above the law, and that they will act as they choose irrespective of what a statute provides.
Freedom and the maintenance of freedom depend on the foundation stone of all law, namely that, whether it be a minister of the crown or a humble individual, all are equal before the law. The fact that a person is a minister of the crown, a position of power under our system, affords no excuse for such a person placing himself, his government,

Combines Investigation Act or the cabinet, above the responsibilities that parliament in its wisdom, and at the request of the government to which he belongs, placed upon the statute books of the country. The issue is far greater than any question as to whether or not there has been wrongdoing on the part of the flour milling companies. I will not now or at any time deal with the facts of a case which may come before the courts and endeavour to pick out excerpts from a report in order to make a case against anybody. Overshadowing the question as to whether or not there was guilt or innocence, or whether Mr. Gordon did or did not make representations, transcending everything, there is what I feel, and what I believe the country as a whole will feel, is a flagrant disregard of parliament. Indeed it is a perpetuation in the days of peace of the centralization of power and authority that was vested in the government. Although such emergency powers no longer exist they have been in this instance exercised by one or more ministers in cabinet council who in their wisdom have decided that an appointee of the people of Canada, carrying out a responsibility under the law, shall not have his recommendations brought before the people because the government has decided that the facts upon which he bases his conclusions are unjustified. My parting word is this. Would parliament even know now that there was a report against the flour milling companies last December if Mr. McGregor had not finally decided that his services could no longer be given to Canada?

Mr. Speaker, today's debate has arisen in an unprecedented fashion. I have been in the house for fourteen years, and during that time I do not remember an occasion upon which, on a motion to go into supply, a minister of the crown has aired a government grievance, because that is what we have been subjected to. I do not propose to traverse the same ground as that which has been so ably covered by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I merely want to say that I agree with him wholeheartedly when he says that no government, no minister, has any right at any time to disregard a statute adopted by parliament, and the provision in that statute for the publication of a report within fifteen days for the information of the people of Canada.
This report was made to the government on December 29, 1948. That is over ten months ago. Today the report was brought into the house at three o'clock, and not one of us had an opportunity to see it until that time. Some of us were busily engaged in the house all afternoon, and the manner in which the report is now before the house

and is being debated will preclude the possibility of its discussion at any time later this session. A debate having arisen on a particular matter, the same subject of debate cannot be raised subsequently in the same session. I know if I had the opportunity, and if it were possible to move another amendment on going into supply, I would be inclined to move a vote of censure on the government for concealing from the house and the people of Canada for ten months a report which they were obligated by statute to make public. Unfortunately, because of the procedure that has been followed, we are prevented from moving any motion whatsoever. I think this house would be justified in defeating the motion and denying the government supply, to show that the house does not intend the country and parliament to be treated in the way the government have treated us on this occasion. After all, when the Combines Investigation Act was before the house in years gone by the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, who was particularly interested in this legislation, and subsequently the minister of justice, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, told the house that the one great weapon upon which the government relied to deal with monopolistic practices, price fixing and combines in this country was publicity. Publicity was the weapon; publicity was almost all that was needed, and prosecution came after publicity. In this case publicity was prevented and, as has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), it is altogether likely that if Mr. McGregor had not submitted his resignation this report would not have been made public today.
Who is Mr. McGregor? He has been one of the outstanding civil servants in this country. Mr. McGregor served the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King years ago, when Mr. Mackenzie King was minister of labour, He served as Mr. Mackenzie King's secretary when he was engaged in the writing of "Industry and Humanity" at the time he was engaged with the Rockefeller Foundation. Mr. McGregor has made a notable contribution to the life and welfare of this country over many years, and I believe in this connection he felt that he would not be doing his public duty if he failed to bring this matter forcibly before the country by placing his resignation in the hands of the government. After all, let us bear in mind what his letter of resignation says. And let me say to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), that although this afternoon a reply to Mr. McGregor's resignation was placed upon the records of this house, when we asked that Mr. McGregor's resignation also be placed upon the record, our

request was denied. I like to see fair play in these matters, and I say that preventing the publication of Mr. McGregor's letter in Hansard while reading Mr. Donald Gordon's reply this afternoon was not fair play at all.
This inquiry was undertaken by Mr. McGregor, or so his letter indicates, with the authority and approval of the minister of justice of that day, Mr. Ilsley. Later on, according to Mr. McGregor, he understood the present minister's opinion to be that this investigation never should have been initiated, though I am prepared to believe that there may be some misunderstanding in that connection. However, it was initiated, and a report has been made. We have had no opportunity to study that report; but during the supper hour-that is, for most of the hon. members of this house; I did not go down to supper-I read this report as quickly as I could; and I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he cannot conceal the practices of these milling companies by talking about the contribution they made during the war. I admit that contribution, but the matters referred to in this report arose long before the war. In 1934 and 1936 these practices of combinations and price fixing were prevalent in this country among the milling interests, and I have no doubt that the same practices are continuing at the present time. I have taken some pages from the record which was produced in this house this afternoon. The report indicates that prior to the war-never mind the war years-by their own admission, by their own memoranda, by their own minutes, by their own communications and correspondence, the milling interests were engaged in price fixing, in maintaining high prices and in trying to destroy the small milling interests of this country. That is writ large in this report from the minutes and records of the milling companies themselves.
I have reason to know that during the war they also had the support of milling interests overseas in their attempt to prevent the development of competitive milling interests in this country. I know perfectly well that the farmers of western Canada established a small co-operative mill just before the war, and that mill found it very difficult to operate during the first year or two of the war because they could not get any overseas orders. They could not sell a barrel of their flour to the British ministry of food; and it was only when the position was drawn to the attention of members of the British parliament, and indeed to the attention of the members of the British government interested in the development of co-operatives, that the condition was righted and the co-operative mill in Saskatchewan
Combines Investigation Act began to receive orders for flour from overseas. I say I know what I am talking about;
I know that is true.
Running all through the evidence submitted in this report by Mr. McGregor is an attempt on the part of the big milling interests not only to control prices, not only to continue their combination and their monopoly, but to destroy the small milling interests of this country. I have in my hand, from chapter 7 of the report, official records of price agreements and discussions. Hon. members will find this record at pages 75 and 76 of the report which was presented this afternoon. Meetings of the organizations to which reference is made were reported in the official minutes by the secretaries, but the principal admissions were found in the records obtained by Mr. McGregor after he obtained access to their memoranda relating to these meetings. Let us look at memorandum No. 28, "Report of sales managers."
The secretary reported that two of the members were exacting only 40 cents per barrel for top patent over the basic grade, instead of 50 cents, in the province of Quebec.
It was unanimously agreed to maintain the 50 cents differential throughout eastern Canada.
There is no record of that in the minutes. Then again:
The following minimum prices were established^ mills pledging themselves to adhere rigidly thereto:
Quebec, $5.75 per barrel . . .
Ontario, $5.65 per barrel . . .
Maritime provinces, $6.75 per barrel . . .
In connection with the maritime provinces, the secretary was instructed to circularize the members, calling attention to the fact that the $6.75 price is applicable only to large jobbers, as well as bakers in Halifax, Saint John and Dartmouth; smaller jobbers to be sold at the spreads indicated in the maritime jobbers' list. The price to dealers to be $7 net.
(Exhibit 577)
There is no reference to that in the minutes. That was in 1938; and on December 14 of the same year we have memorandum No. 33, "Small mill competition in western Canada."
One of the members reported on the discussion which took place in Winnipeg, December 9, at which time it was thought that whatever line of action was deemed necessary should be confined to those areas in which small mills are particularly active, and the suggestions then offered were the making of a special price in those areas and, if necessary, the introduction of a special brand. The question to receive the further consideration of western managers in meeting early in the new year. The two members engaged in the sale of flour in western Canada and not represented at the meeting were requested to communicate with their western managers.
What did the minutes say? No record in the minutes of this vital decision.
It was reported that a meeting would be held in the new year at which western sales managers would be present.

Combines Investigation Act
That is the statement in the minutes, but there is no reference to the attempt to establish a new brand to sell at a low price in order to undersell the small mills in western Canada and put them out of business. There you have at least one reason why this combination should be prosecuted by the government. Never mind the years of the war. What were they doing before the war and what have they been doing since? It is that question which hon. gentlemen should ask themselves.
In eastern Canada the same attempt was being made. Efforts were made to get the small mills to adhere to the price-fixing policy of the large mills. Those efforts are reflected in some extracts I shall read from letters passing between Mr. C. H. G. Short and Mr. J. J. Page, on August 31, 1938. We were not at war then and these companies were not performing any war service at that time. At page 91 of the report we find the following:
If McCarthy continues as he Is continuing, and I think the point should be stressed strongly to him, it will be a very short while now before the big mills are meeting his competition right in his own bailiwick, which will mean that the rest of the small mills, and the big mills themselves, are in for a protracted period of unremunerative business. Surely he has sense enough to see that with a discretion below a maintained price of the large mills he is infinitely better off than he can possibly be by setting his own price levels-which will inevitably be met, countered and possibly bettered by some of the big mills within a very short time il he persists.
This should interest some of the Ontario members. The correspondence makes it clear that the competition from the Copeland Milling Company, whose plant is located at Midland, Ontario, was regarded as of particular importance to the milling combine. Here is an extract from a memorandum of decisions reached at an executive meeting on April 5, 1939.
It was unanimously agreed to institute special price reductions at irregular intervals on the following basis:
As a trial, the reduction shall be applicable to bakers in all towns located on or south of the branch line of the C.N.R. running from Belleville west to Midland, Ontario; and the price to be applicable to jobbers in this territory on their purchases of baker-flour requirements in jute.
It is understood that the reduction will be agreed upon at irregular intervals, at the discretion of the mills.
This is cat and mouse business. Lower and raise your prices at irregular intervals, then finally destroy the small miller.
The frequency and amount of the reduction in price shall be mutually agreed upon between the mills on a majority vote of four members. The reduction to be effected, and the time of its coming into effect, shall be made known to all members as soon after the market close on a Friday as is possible.

The period of the reduction shall be from the market close on Friday agreed upon until the following Tuesday morning at the opening of the Winnipeg market, after which time no further business shall be accepted at the reduced price.
At the discretion of the mills, the reduction may apply to any or all classes of trade in any one or more of the eastern provinces.
So, we can go on with records of that kind of combination and that sort of attempt to destroy a competitor by underselling him.
Mr. J. J. Page (Western Canada) expressed himself as follows in a letter to Mr. Charles Ritz of the Robin Hood Company in Minneapolis. It is dated September 29, 1938, which is before the war.
There seems to be a sharp difference of opinion in the west as to how to combat the small mills . . .
It is true that the country mills are quite keen competitors of the larger mills, and have been giving us quite a bit of trouble, but I do not think we can do other than accept the recommendation of our western men who, with one exception, say we should maintain our present grades and our relative selling bases.
In this report you find evidence that before the war these things were being done. This afternoon the minister tried to brush off Mr. McGregor's criticism and his conclusions by talking about the war years and what Mr. McGregor learned during those war years. As a matter of fact this report is replete with references to the millers' combination and the millers' price-fixing trust in the years before the war.
Mr. McGregor said a careful examination had been made of all the evidence and memoranda. I think that is true because, after all, it is not in the minutes but in the memoranda existing in their offices that one finds the damning indictment which has been brought against these powerful milling interests. The small mills worried them all the time. We have a memorandum of an executive meeting on April 14, 1936, which reads as follows:
It was understood that the discretion of ten cents per barrel in the maritime provinces heretofore enjoyed by Messrs. Ogilvies, would be removed. Messrs. Ogilvies gave the above assurance on the understanding that their position in respect to small mill competition is quite clear, i.e., that they were not concerned here or there about the odd car of flour, but that they would take whatever steps were necessary to hold their old and established connections against the competition of small mills.
Throughout this report there is evidence of the attempt to cut out competition. I should like to ask my friends of the Liberal party how this fits with their allegiance to free competition or free enterprise, if you like. We find this government, which is pledged to maintain free enterprise in this country, has for ten months concealed a report which was a condemnation of big interests which were crushing out free competition. My hon. friend

from Winnipeg North Centre reminds me that the government was breaking the law in order to do just that.
Then there is a memorandum of the executive dated February 20, 1936, which suggests that an advance or decline in the price of feed would be governed by a vote of the majority. Then there is a memorandum, No. 5, reporting a somewhat similar meeting on June 9, 1936, just a few months later. It reads in part as follows:
It was resolved that the domestic price on feed shall be governed by the highest ruling price on the North American continent.
That is 1936, when the farmers were down and out and when their stock was almost worthless. These gentlemen get together and resolve that the domestic prices on feed shall be governed by the highest ruling price on the continent of North America.
The minutes of the meeting of Ontario sales managers dated December 14, 1938, was concerned with an understanding about much the same matter.
. . . that the secretary would consult the Montreal members each week to determine a minimum selling price for feeds, which minimum selling level would be based on export feed values.
Everywhere you look in this report- whether it be the war years or the years at which I have been looking, particularly, because I do not intend to deal with the war years tonight-you find the same thing: maintain the highest possible price, get rid of your competitors, and discipline any member of the milling interests that will not agree with you.
On July 21, 1939, they made some price changes: Exhibit 441.
"Price Changes:
Present prices are taken as being promulgated on No. 2 northern cash wheat 50 cents per bushel, and shall advance 15 cents per barrel for each 2 cents per bushel advance up to 60 cents; and shall be reduced 10 cents per barrel for each 3 cents per bushel decline in the market; always making allowance for millfeed changes."
The reason for this change is outlined in a letter of July 24, 1939, from C. H. G. Short (Lake of the Woods) -
I think he was mentioned this afternoon;
I think he was the gentleman who was in charge of this particular field under the wartime prices and trade board during the war.
-to G. H. Booth of the Winnipeg office:
"I also managed to sneak a gentle suggestion over, which was adopted-that with every 2 cents upward movement until the No. 2 wheat reached the 60 cent price the price should be advanced 15 cents and that price should be reduced 10 cents per barrel only on decline of 3 cents per bushel. This arrangement, I hope, will mean that with movement in the market we will get in an even better position than the $3.30 price legislated."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Quite a sneak.
Combines Investigation Act

There again you have the type of thing that was done by these powerful companies.
I cannot go into all the matters because there are several other things I want to say; but whether they were dealing with the bakers, with government institutions, or the Department of Justice purchasing for the penitentiaries before the war, or whether they were provisioning Canadian government ships, they all got together, and they decided what they would do about it together. In other words, they acted as a combination; they controlled prices; they set prices; and this report is replete with evidence in that regard. Then we are told that this report was unsatisfactory to the government, that it was not the kind of report which should be made public, and the commissioner resigned because he was determined that the people of Canada should know what was going on.
During the 1930's, when the province from which I come was the victim of the most unprecedented drought in our history, we find indeed the first letter which Mr. McGregor says is evidence of this price fixing, of September 15, 1936, from D. P. Noel to
J.	Sangster (Western Canada) Winnipeg. He says:
"I confirm my telephone conversation with you this afternoon during which I indicated I had received confirmation from all mills-
I would call attention to those words "all mills."
-that the municipality at Frontier would be quoted on the basis of $6.10 per barrel for a carlot of first patent flour in cottons, sight draft attached to bill of lading."
Those of us who know where Frontier is know that that flour went down into an area which was one of the worst drought-stricken areas in Saskatchewan.
The same thing applied to millfeeds. When millfeeds were being sent into British Columbia, evidently some of the people who sold millfeeds in that province were not maintaining the prices laid down. In 1944, as you will find throughout the war years, complaints were made that the price ceiling was not observed. Bear this in mind, and let us be clear about it. The price ceiling as laid down during the war was a ceiling, never a floor and was never intended to be a floor. This is the reference I am going to make to those war years. You will find that throughout the war years these milling interests insisted on maintaining the highest prices permitted by the government, with a few notable exceptions. They kept at the ceiling and all kept the same price; and
1512	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act when one of them broke away, then of course there was a good deal of criticism of that one by the rest of the combine.
A special system of quotation was adopted at Vancouver which illustrates exactly what I mean. The proposed procedure at Vancouver-and this is a wartime matter-was outlined in a letter of June 8, 1944, from Mr. J. Clark, Vancouver, secretary of the Vancouver group, to Mr. Noel in which he said this:
''Following receipt of the directive issued by you on the subject of tenders of the Department of Munitions and Supply, a meeting of the Vancouver members was held to discuss and draw up a plan to give effect to the suggestion therein contained. As a result the following was agreed upon,-
I may say that I am not going to read the story on the previous page, but they were having trouble with a Vancouver group, the name of which I have forgotten at the moment, which was offering flour and so on at a lower price than they had agreed upon. The letter continues:

This whole business revives in my mind the memory of the relationship which we in Alberta had with Mr. McGregor some years ago in connection with an alleged combine in restraint of the tobacco trade. I was a member of the Alberta government at the time and I recall a visit I made to Ottawa early in 1938 when I had a discussion with Mr. McGregor. He urged us in the strongest possible way to take action in the province of Alberta, we being one of the provinces

where it was patently clear that a combine did exist, in order to bring the whole matter to the attention of the Canadian people.

As a result of Mr. McGregor's report on the alleged combine in the distribution of tobacco products which was issued on August 31, 1938, the province of Alberta took action. They prepared well and long and spent over $50,000 in an effort to obtain convictions under the Combines Investigation Act. However, that act made it absolutely impossible to get convictions even though there was every evidence in the opinion of many legal persons in the province that it was an open and shut case.
We found Mr. McGregor to be, not only a faithful but a courageous public servant, a man who took his duties seriously. We respected him and his judgment and his advice. It seems too bad that his career should end in the way it has. I feel practically certain that if we were to have a full-dress debate on this report such a thing would be brought to light. I fully believe that that is the case.
I just want to join with what the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said since I came into the house at eight o'clock, and also with what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, and to protest in the strongest possible way against the manner in which the government has handled this whole business. The Minister of Justice called me on the telephone just before three o'clock and said he would like to see me. I told him I would be in my room and he came up to my room. He said that he did not want to suggest that I should not ask the question, but that he wanted to give me some facts before I would ask it. The facts that he gave me were that the government had a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act ready and did not want to make any report public before that bill was passed.
I am not a member of the official opposition, but I am on the opposition side of the house. I never considered that it was my duty to use every opportunity I could get to embarrass the government. I considered that it was my duty, so far as possible, to help the government give good government to Canada. I did not want to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) anything in my office that I would not ask him on the floor of the house. Therefore I did not even ask him if there was a report. I asked him-and remember this was on the 21st of September-when the bill would be introduced. He said, in ten days or two weeks. Room 122, Justice Building, October 29, 1949
Hon. Stuart S. Garson,
Minister of Justice,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Garson:
I should appreciate it if I could be relieved of my duties as commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act at an early date. I hope my resignation can be effective not later than December 31 next,
I hope that within the next few weeks X can complete the two reports which are now in draft form. But if an earlier date would be more satisfactory to you, I shall of course be prepared to retire at whatever time you say.
It is a keen disappointment to me to feel obliged to withdraw, before my time, from work which I am convinced can be made of great service to the public of Canada, work which has been my chief interest during the past twenty-four years and in which I have had the whole-hearted co-operation of a group of very competent and public-spirited associates.
The occasion for my taking this step is briefly indicated in the attached memorandum.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me the privilege of reading the memorandum, since it is a part of the case in the same way as the memorandum prepared by Mr. Donald Gordon which was read in the house this afternoon. The memorandum is dated October 29, 1949, and reads:
Memorandum to
The Minister of Justice:
The principal circumstances which have led me to submit my resignation as commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act can be stated briefly.
First and foremost is my deep concern about certain tendencies that have been apparent in recent months which in my opinion seriously threaten the usefulness of this legislation.
One of the principal remedial measures provided by the Combines Investigation Act is the publication of reports of investigations. The withholding for so many months of publication of a report which the act requires shall be made public as soon as possible after its receipt (this is the only instance of the kind in my experience) is one illustration of the tendencies I have in mind.
Closely related to this are the differences of opinion on basic policy that have been revealed in our recent discussions relating to the flour investigation and report. I am not raising any question of your obvious right and the right of anyone to point out errors in any work I have done. The criticisms made, however, have not been directed particularly to any error of fact in my report but primarily to the policy that was followed. You have expressed the opinion that the inquiry should never have been started. I am satisfied in my own mind that the facts disclosed in the report more than justify the investigation.
May I just stop there to ask who, having listened even to the few facts placed on record this evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), will dare
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
rise in his place in this house and say that the facts already disclosed do not justify the investigation and report.
It was instituted and conducted, as our other inquiries have been, in keeping with the letter and spirit of the act. The conclusions reached, I am convinced, are completely justified and are in keeping with the many judicial interpretations of the statute in other cases. The investigation was started with the knowledge and approval of the then Minister of Justice, Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley. The action we took was in accord with the basic purposes of the act and with my understanding of the government's expressly stated policy of preventing restrictive practices which deprive the public of the benefit of reasonably free competitive conditions.
Just at this point may I refer to the letter of December 29, 1948, which accompanied the report, in which Mr. McGregor said:
Mr. John G. Ahem, K.C., of Montreal, who was appointed by the Minister of Justice to act as counsel in the investigation, conducted the examination of witnesses throughout the hearings, and I wish to acknowledge the able services which he has rendered.
Here is a government that helped the combines investigator make an investigation; then, after he presents his report, they bury it. Now I continue with the memorandum:
I recognize fully that the making of policy is not the responsibility of a civil servant, but as a civil servant I would prefer not to carry on under conditions of uncertainty and conflicting tendencies such as I have experienced recently.
Evidently he did not know under which minister he was supposed to be working.
There is greater need now for strong action under the combines act than there has been at any time in the past twenty-five years. To an alarming degree price fixing activities such as we reported in the flour milling industry have been developing in the post-war years; some of them originated in the war period; and some were started, as in the flour milling industry, even in the pre-war years. To meet the situation, to prevent these practices which are designed to limit or eliminate the public safeguard of price competition, there is every reason why the powers of the combines act should be strengthened. Council accepted in the present bill our proposals of three amendments, including a very important amendment designed to meet the difficulties of the dental judgment, but the only suggestions from council which you called on me to consider seriously were provisions which would have had the result of limiting the effectiveness of the legislation.
I wonder if there is any relation between that phrase and Mr. McGregor's resignation.
I have in mind such proposals as those to eliminate the commissioner's initiative in launching inquiries, to place serious limitations on the requirement that reports be made public, and to provide for exemption, after prior approval, of certain types of agreements to restrict production or eliminate price competition. These suggestions have not been included in the present bill, but my understanding from you is that consideration of them has been merely postponed pending a proposed "overhauling" of the act. Overhauling of the act could serve many useful purposes. I am apprehensive, however, particularly in view of the nature of the changes which have been suggested

for consideration, of the ultimate result of any revision of the statute which would include changes along these or similar lines.
My hope is that my successor, in carrying out responsibilities which have many quasi-judicial aspects and call for a substantial measure of independent action and judgment, will have the support of an even stronger statute than the act in its present form, and a clear statement of government policy with respect to its enforcement.
I do not believe there is much more I can usefully add; but I want to tell members of this house, wherever they sit, that this is a matter which comes before loyalty to the government. It concerns loyalty to the people of Canada. If by your silence or otherwise you approve the policy the government followed in this instance, then I can tell the people of this country that their interests have very little safeguard if that safeguard lies with the present government.
