Wilson Boxes Limited, the new trial of one accused in Rex v. Container Materials, conviction and no appeal taken; Rex v. Badden et al., shipping containers, fines and no appeal taken; finally Rex v. Ash-Temple, the dental supplies case, in which there was an acquittal, which has come under the criticism of my hon. friend from Lake Centre.
I believe that those cases I have recited indicate that, in matters of very great complexity and difficulty, the batting average of this department and of this government in connection with these prosecutions has been unusually high.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: And of Mr. McGregor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, indeed.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Why did you not go ahead with this case, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend's interjection is fortunate in that it leads up to a point I wanted to make. My hon. friend, the member for Lake Centre, suggests that this government conspired to instruct counsel in such a way that the case would be bungled and the accused freed. I should like to place on record the fact that, in connection with the instructions to counsel in the Ash-Temple case, the dental supplies case, ever since I came into the department I have been under the impression-I confirmed it an hour ago with Mr. McGregor-that Mr. McGregor had a free hand in recommending the selection of counsel. This was true in most of these cases. As a matter of fact, the man who was selected was recommended to him, and through him to the government, by Mr. Peter White of Toronto, an eminent and able man himself. He suggested we should have as counsel Mr. D. L. McCarthy, K.C., one of the outstanding counsel in Canada.
I notice my hon. friend nods his head in agreement.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Will the minister permit one question? In the other cases in which prosecution was successful, were the documents put in without proof of names and without proof of authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
That is an extremely ingenious question. My hon. friend says, in relation to over fifteen cases I have listed, and the details of which neither he nor I have ever seen, could I tell him whether, in my opinion, this or that or the other was proven? I can tell him I have not the faintest idea.
That brings me to this dental supplies case which has an important bearing upon the matter which is now before this house. After having been sworn in on November 15, I was faced with the necessity of securing a seat in a by-election, so I did not come to Ottawa to carry on the duties of minister until the early part of January, this year. One of a number of matters which I found upon my desk at that time was the report of the combines investigation commissioner in connection with the flour milling industry. I should like to lay before you, Mr. Speaker, and through you, before the members of the house, the situation as I then found it. I took this report which was upon my desk- a report which had not been delivered to me in person because I was not here to receive it, upon a matter about which I had no more personal information than I have about the present state of affairs in Siam- I took this report to cabinet for discussion with my colleagues and I hope I can discuss this matter without breaking any cabinet secrets. When I took it in for discussion with my colleagues, I was at once confronted with

the viewpoint that, with regard to the war years, the tenor of this report was quite contrary to the understanding upon which the wartime prices and trade board had operated. Not having been in the government during the period of price control, who was I to question that viewpoint of my colleagues? And I would never have questioned it in any event.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Whom were you confronted by?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: You could have read the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
But that was not all. We had this sincere difference of opinion, which has been so sincere upon the part of one of the parties that he has resigned his position as a result of it and which is just as sincere, may I say, on the part of those who hold the opposite view. But in the carrying out of my duties as Minister of Justice I was not only confronted with this basic difference of opinion on some of the most important facts with which the report dealt, but I was also confronted at the same time with a great state of uncertainty with regard to the law that was to be applicable to those facts.
The dental supplies case had been heard by Mr. Justice Barlow with a jury on March 18, 1948. In that case, upon the ground that the documents were alleged to have been found in the possession of the employees and agencies of the corporate accused and were tendered in evidence upon that basis, and upon the basis that incriminating documents found in the possession of the accused are binding on the accused, the trial judge in the early stages of the trial permitted these documents to be entered as evidence. Later he withdrew the case from the jury upon the ground that there was not sufficient evidence upon which a jury could render a verdict. That was in March, 1948.
This group of counsel whom my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) accuses of being derelict, fumbling and neglectful-

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I never said that the counsel were derelict. I said that the government departed from the regular principles of proving ordinary documents in the ordinary way, and directed these counsel to act as they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Having a little while ago
given me credit for being a mind-reader, the hon. member now shows great propensities in that direction himself.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I never gave the minister credit for being a mind-reader or anything else.
Combines Investigation Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: My hon. friend knows perfectly well, as a leading counsel himself, that counsel who is in charge of a case of this kind is the man who determines what evidence he is going to put in; and no clients, least of all experienced clients like Mr. McGregor and his associates in the combines investigation department, would ever think of instructing their lawyer as to the legal methods of proof. They take advice from him as to what evidence the lawyers wish them to adduce. What my hon. friend is doing, although he may want to take away from it now, is this-

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: He does not want to take away anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
What it amounts to is this. He is accusing counsel in that case of gross neglect of duty and gross carelessness in the presentation of their case. I say on behalf of the government that we accepted, as we had in previous instances, the recommendation of the combines investigation department as to the identity of counsel. Unlike my hon. friend, we have no great complaint as regards counsel. Our complaint is with regard to the judgment which was given, and which we are now attempting to correct in the bill which is on the order paper.
At any rate, in March, 1948, the trial judge withdrew the case from the jury and said that there was no evidence to go before the jjry. From that judgment our counsel appealed. The appeal came on and was discussed before the court of appeal from September 27 to October 13,	1948. The
argument on the appeal took that length of time because of the fact that hundreds of exhibits were presented and complex legal issues were brought before the court by both sides of the argument on appeal. Following the hearing or argument, the court of appeal reserved judgment.
Thus in the early part of January, when I came here as Minister of Justice, I had on my desk a report in respect of which on some of the most basic facts there was a strong difference of opinion amongst highly intelligent and sincere people. I was also confronted with a state of the law which, if it was to be considered to be as it was held to be in the trial court judgment delivered in March, 1948, or as set out in the argument on behalf of the accused in the appeal court hearing in September and October, 1948, would leave us in an extremely difficult position in proving our case, quite regardless of this difference of opinion as to the facts.
It was not until February 28, the last day of February, 1949, that the appeal court of Ontario which had heard this case in September and October of 1948, delivered
4578]-97

Combines Investigation Act their judgment. We have never disguised- and certainly I have never disguised-or made any attempt to disguise the fact that that judgment is a body blow against the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. When the hon. member for Lake Centre says that the bill we are bringing forward now to undo the effects of that judgment just deals with a trifling little matter, he is showing a much smaller knowledge of the law than I should have thought he possessed.
While I do not want to anticipate my own legislation in any way, I think it is essential that I should say a few words about the issue which was raised in this case, because it is impossible to understand the position in which the government has been placed unless one understands the effect of the dental supplies judgment upon the very issue of the flour-milling report that we are discussing this evening.
We have two other sections in this bill, but the real necessity for introducing this amending legislation at the present time is because of the uncertainty of the law, a situation which has been created by this decision of the Ontario court of appeal of February, 1949. Following that decision the first thing we did -and this took considerable time-was to obtain the legal opinion from Mr. D. L. McCarthy, K.C., our leading counsel, concerning the judgment in question, so that we might on the basis of such opinion, and in further consultation with him, draft an amendment which would offset the effect of this judgment. I think the first draft of the amendment was made on April 7, 1949. As hon. members who were in the former parliament know that was at a time when there certainly was no prospect of securing any amendment to the Combines Investigation Act in that session of parliament. The amendment we are now submitting has been reached only after several drafts have been made since this first one. In the course of making those drafts we have dealt with a number of suggestions coming from Mr. McGregor and his associates. As he correctly enough says in his letter that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) read into the record tonight, we also dealt with certain suggestions which came from the cabinet. Under the act Mr. McGregor has extremely wide powers. I do not think there is any other civil servant in Canada who has much wider powers than Mr. McGregor has under the act. He has the power to initiate all inquiries without any reference to any minister at all. In most cases he carried on a preliminary investigation. I believe that the ratio of cases in which final report is made to the total of the preliminary investigations is

about 10 per cent. In other words it is only in the more serious cases that he conducts a complete inquiry and files a report.
Mr. McGregor refers to my predecessor, the Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley, as having authorized these proceedings to go forward, but Mr. Ilsley's giving authority had nothing but academic significance, because his authority was not required. The commissioner himself has complete authority to go forward without authority from the minister. To charge the government that places in the hands of one of its civil servants that measure of authority with neglect in this matter seems to me to be somewhat unreasonable.
But, sir, notwithstanding this very great authority which the commissioner has, we in the cabinet like to feel that we have a small residue of responsibility, if I may speak jocularly, for matters of policy.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Get the authority from parliament then to have that responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: You should do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: What I meant was we have some responsibility to initiate ideas, to have ideas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: The hon. member may not like that.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I was talking about withholding the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: No; I meant to have ideas.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: We are glad to know you have them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
We had a number of ideas from Mr. McGregor and his associates, in respect to the formation of which he was under no restrictions whatever. Any good ideas that occurred to them they put down and sent to me and I took them into cabinet. There were no restrictions whatever. Well, we had a few ideas ourselves, and we, with some timidity in view of the great powers that the commissioner had, ventured to put these forward, and he turned every one of them down. These are the ones he refers to in his letter.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that in the legislation which is now before the house there is not one syllable but what came from Mr. McGregor and his associates.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: He says so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, that is right. But more than that, to every single one of those ideas that we had he said, "I object to them". We said, "All right, Mr. McGregor, we won't press them". And that is the way the matter stood.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Surely not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: The main section of the bill deals with this difficulty that had arisen in the dental supplies case. In that case, as in all of these cases, I think it requires no great amount of imagination on the part of hon. members to realize, if they stop to think about the matter at all, that when you send the mounted police into a man's business and pick up the documents that he might regard as having some potential embarrassment to him, and take them away and make them the basis of a prosecution, the prospect of getting him or his associates or employees to testify on behalf of the crown or to co-operate with any great amount of enthusiasm or zeal is not very great. Therefore when you get down to the practical job of proving your case you have to rely pretty heavily upon the principle of law which is known as the possessory principle which is that if a man is charged with conspiracy, any documents of an incriminating nature which may be found in his possession are evidence against him. We have applied that principle, which applies to individuals also, to accused corporations. I want to enter a reservation here, Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer. I am giving a very oversimplified application of the law in order to make myself more thoroughly understood. In all of these cases we have attempted, and in several of them successfully, to apply to corporations the possessory principle which certainly is not disputed at all as regards individuals. We did that in cases which I have here. Rex v. Simington, 1926, 43 C.C.C. 249 was one of them. Rex v. Container Materials Limited et al., 1940, 4 D.L.R. 293, was another. We were successful in these cases in producing the documents and filing them as exhibits and contending that because they were found in the corporate possession of the accused corporation therefore they were evidence against that corporation. It was in very large measure upon the basis of that evidence that we were able to secure a conviction.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Is that case reported?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend. When we did the same thing in the dental supplies case the court, both the trial court and the court of appeal, rejected that evidence. They rejected it upon the basis of a principle which we contend is newly enunciated, and which we think should be cured by the amendments which we are now proposing if we are ever to have an enforceable act.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Why did the minister not go to the Supreme Court of Canada with that case?
45781-97J
Combines Investigation Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will just permit me to finish a rather complicated subject without interrupting me with questions I should appreciate it.
What Chief Justice Robertson of Ontario said in that case was this:
The proof required, however, in the case of a company differs somewhat from that required in the case of an individual. If the act relied on is that of an officer, servant or agent of the company, there must be evidence that he had authority from the company to perform the act. Mere possession of a document by the company, in the sense that the document was on its premises, or even in the company's files, may not, without more, afford ground for an inference that its contents had come to the knowledge of its board of directors, or of someone having authority from the company to deal with the matters to which the document relates.
At a later point in the same judgment His Lordship said:
There is, however, one objection common to all the letters. There is no evidence that the writing of any of them was authorized by any of the accused companies, nor is there evidence that anyone having authority to bind the company had any knowledge of the sending of any of the letters or of their receipt or of their contents.
These combines investigation cases usually are based largely upon documents picked up by the mounted police or by other agents of the combines investigation commission from the possession of the various alleged accused. One, two, three or a dozen of the documents in themselves may not spell out the nature of the offence; but all of a large number when put together like a complicated jigsaw puzzle so that they all fit in can build up a case. But if in relation to each one of the documents we had to prove that the board of directors had a meeting and authorized the document to be written, or that some person in the company having authority had authorized that to be done which was set out in the document, we would have an extremely difficult time to ever prove a case at all where offences of this nature had been committed.
Hon. members can understand that where you are dealing with a trade association made up of all the firms in one industry, you are dealing with an entity that is not incorporated and which cannot be joined as a party defendant. You may not want to prosecute the underlings who have the actual handling of association matters. Unless you can rely upon the possessory principle as regards the corporate accused it would be extremely difficult in some cases to secure a conviction.
That is why we are bringing forward this amendment. That is one reason why we wished not to act upon the flour report or to publish it until we had our legislation in shape.

Combines Investigation Act
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) says that that is inconsistent with the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I suppose it is, but he is not the Minister of Justice; he has not my responsibility.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
If mere consistency was our aim, it would be a simple matter, as the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree, he being a lawyer of some note, to have had all the evidence and all the witnesses agree exactly with mathematical certainty. But the fact is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had an opinion in relation to this matter based upon his viewpoint as Minister of Trade and Commerce and his experience during the war which I could not possibly share because I was in another activity altogether at that time. I have my own viewpoint in relation to this matter which largely centred around this question.
How were we going to deal with this report that was on my desk in a way that would bring a reasonable amount of credit to or how were we going to avoid bringing discredit to the combines investigation administration and the government? If with these differences of opinion as to the basic facts, with this uncertainty as to the condition of the law, we had published the report and if the counsel of the flour milling companies had shown one-quarter the capacity or had adopted one-quarter of the shrewd tactics of the defence lawyers in the dental supplies case, they would have said, "All right, go ahead and prosecute; we challenge you to prosecute." Then on the condition of the facts and on the condition of the law we would have had what the hon. member for Lake Centre referred to as another debacle on our hands. Then he would have got up and waggled his finger at us and denounced us for having- he did it today without any cause whatever- in effect conspired with counsel whom we had instructed to so conduct the prosecutions that we would never get convictions. We do not do business in that way.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: You just hide the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: My hon. friend asks whether this report would have ever seen the light of day if Mr. McGregor had not resigned. What kind of morons does he take us for in this house? Does he think that any government would have a report of this sort and attempt to stifle it permanently?

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Surely not. Our position is a simple one. We had this report. I do not mind saying that a responsible journalist of
'Mr Garson.]

this city came to me in a friendly way and told me that he did not know whether we had the report or not, but that if we had it and published it, from what he had heard the minute that was done we would be challenged to prosecute. I did not need to be told that.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: When was that that the minister was so informed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That would be some time in the spring of 1949.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Just before the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, it was before; that is right. But not just before, and I do not know the political persuasion of that journalist.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: We can suspect.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Give us his name and we will tell you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Looking at the matter in retrospect I do not think that the action taken has been contrary to the public interest.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Just the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If we get our amendment we will certainly be in a far better position as regards this or any other report than we are in now. I am going to base my request for support of the amendment on the position that I would not take the responsibility of prosecuting on any report unless we have this amendment. It would be a matter of grave difficulty. When I say that, I hope the hon. member for Lake Centre will get up and give us some support and not describe this amendment as he did today as being a matter of no consequence, just a trifling matter we are dealing with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I must inform the minister that his time has expired.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Go ahead.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: With the unanimous consent of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I have a number of arguments to meet, but I shall try to bring my remarks to a quick conclusion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Do not forget to answer the three speeches from down here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I shall try to do that without offending too greatly against the rules of the house. I do not intend to deal with the report because I assume that all hon. members are literate and can read it themselves. The report speaks for itself.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Before the minister goes on to deal with the other speeches may I ask him just one question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will ask his question after I have dealt with the other matters, it would be better. If I am not careful I shall not have any time left.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: The minister is going on to other matters. My simple question is this: What justification in law or otherwise does the minister have for departing from the mandatory responsibility placed upon him by the statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I thought I had attempted during the course of the past few minutes to answer the very question my hon. friend has asked, but if I have not answered it to his satisfaction I shall not make any further effort to do so. As I say, I do not want to deal with the report because I think it speaks for itself, but there are one or two points that have not been brought out which I think deserve to be mentioned.
First of all, there is no allegation in the report of any breach of the act at all after decontrol came into effect. The evidence indicates that the occasion for the investigation being started in the first place was that upon decontrol Mr. McGregor, who is a very diligent and conscientious man in the discharging of his duty, saw that-it was in September, 1947, if I remember correctly- there was a uniform price rise in flour and mill feed put into effect at the same time by all the main milling companies. As I think is quite proper, he formed the hypothesis that this might be some indication of a breach of the act. He went to Mr. Taylor, who was then chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, to find out why these prices had gone up uniformly in this way. This is a rather condensed version, but what he was told was this. Mr. Taylor said that the government, greatly concerned with the large increase in the price of flour, and particularly in the price of mill feed, in the United States, was as anxious as they could be to avoid a similar increase in Canada. Although their legal powers under the wartime prices and trade board had expired with decontrol, Mr. Taylor was instructed to go to Mr. Short, the flour controller, and tell him that the government would look with extreme disfavour on any undue increase in the price of flour and mill feed upon decontrol, and that it was desired that the inevitable increase which would take place at that time should be kept to a minimum.
With that in view Mr. Taylor went to Mr. Short, and Mr. Short was prevailed upon ;o get his own company, the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, to increase the price of flour and of mill feed by a considerably smaller figure than he was disposed to, very
Combines Investigation Act much smaller than some of the other companies were disposed to, and to a very, very much smaller price than then prevailed in the United States. The suggestion was that, although the legal powers to enforce these arrangements had expired, if there were not reasonable co-operation in the matter the government would have to consider taking powers again to achieve that result.
This request was accepted under protest. Mr. Taylor told me that he even had a man call him up from Montreal and say, "What is the matter with you men? You are not satisfied with pushing us around all through the war; when the war is over and all your legal powers have expired you still have that zeal to push us around and threaten us with the renewal of controls you have just taken off." After considerable remonstrance and discussion the millers accepted $4.05 for flour and a price of $10 for mill feed, the desire being that the price of flour should not be held down at the cost of having mill feed rise too high. The reference in Mr. McGregor's letter to my having said that the inquiry should never have been started was based on that episode, and upon the information given to me by Mr. Taylor in the presence of Mr. McGregor and Mr. Gordon in my office. I said that what Mr. Taylor had told me, as he had told Mr. McGregor in September, 1947, seemed to me, in the absence of some other evidence of an improper agreement, a pretty reasonable explanation which would account for the uniform increase in the price of flour and mill feed. If it be taken, as I think it is reasonable that it should be, that this increase in price of September, 1947, was a price increase initiated and directed by the government through Mr. Taylor with a view to holding down the inevitable increase upon decontrol to a reasonable figure, then that was not an agreement at all let alone an improper one. Since that time, according to the report there has not been any evidence whatever of any breach of the act.
So far as the wartime period is concerned,
I wonder whether there is a general understanding as to the nature of the arrangements that were made with the milling industry in connection with the operations of the wartime prices and trade board. At the risk of belabouring a point that has already been touched upon, perhaps I might be permitted to attempt to oversimplify it in these terms. When a price ceiling was put on all products there was one notable exception, and that was the price of wheat. The price of wheat was permitted to rise at the same time that the price of flour was under a price ceiling. Of course if you increase the cost of your raw material and do not increase the price of your

Combines Investigation Act finished product, the people engaged in turning out the finished product are bound to be squeezed against the ceiling. The millers' suggestion was a fine one. They said: We have no objection to the price of wheat rising, but let the price of flour go up along with it and we will be perfectly satisfied. Of course, apart from all other considerations, that could not be entertained for the reason that a break in the price of flour would have broken the whole price ceiling.
In order to deal with the situation created by a rising cost for wheat and a fixed ceiling for flour, the government stepped in and said: We will pay a subsidy in respect of the cost of wheat to the milling companies upon the condition, however, that the milling industry must accept a limitation of profit clause in this arrangement under which they will be permitted only their standard profits in the pre-war period which, as it happened, were rather low. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said this afternoon, the milling companies had a full 100 per cent excess profits tax under that arrangement. They did not even get the 20 per cent rebate as other industries did. The result of all that was, as long as that arrangement was in effect, if the milling companies sold their flour for less money to the consumer, say 50 cents a bag, the 50 cents came right out of the federal treasury.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, yes.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Out of the taxpayers' pockets.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
That is right. I accept the correction with excellent grace. It is not a bad idea to remember the taxpayers once in a while. It came right out of the taxpayers' pockets. The iniquities charged against the milling companies during this period of control are that they did not sell at prices below the ceiling. If they had done so, every time they had sold below the ceiling price it would have meant an increase in the subsidy they got out of the public treasury or, as my hon. friend says, from the taxpayers. So while there may be accusations that the milling companies charged the ceiling price during that period, and so on, I have never been able to get through my head what purpose there would be behind such alleged irregularities. They could not make a five-cent piece by charging any more for their flour or feed, since the more they charged the less they received in subsidies. If they charged less they would get more subsidies paid by the taxpayers. The milling companies were just a conduit through which benefits flowed or did not flow to the consumer from the treasury or if you like, the taxpayers. The

milling companies themselves could not make or lose anything at all under this arrangement made by the wartime prices and trade board.
My hon. friend asks, what about the period before the war. In that respect the report speaks for itself, but I would point out that this is now a matter of some ten years. If you look up the Criminal Code you will see that even a charge of treason against His Majesty is subject to a three-year limitation. In other words if a man has committed treason previous to that three-year period, nothing can be done about it. So I rather think it is going pretty far back to take proceedings in respect of something done ten years ago. That is quite apart from a point which all the lawyers present will appreciate, that the further back you go in a prosecution, the greater becomes the difficulty of securing evidence and proving your case. I think any person who has had any practical experience in prosecutions knows that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I have trespassed greatly upon the time of the house, but I should like to conclude my remarks by saying this. Notwithstanding the eloquent and able arguments that have been put up by members of the opposition I do not admit that the government has been guilty of an error of judgment in this matter. In the light of the facts and the position of the law, which position will remain until we cure it by the amendments now before the house, it seems to me that the course we followed was not by any means a wholly imprudent one. But if as our opponents argue it was an error in judgment it was a judgment which was reached after the most careful and heart-searching consideration, and on a perfectly honest basis.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRARY VICTORIA. B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is only fair to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that I should go a little further than he has gone. He has valiantly undertaken to accept full responsibility for what was done in this matter. I must say that at various times since the hon. gentleman became Minister of Justice he discussed with me the matters he has placed before the house this evening, the difficulties that arose out of the pending judgment of the Ontario court of appeals in the dental supply case, and the fact that if he published this report he would be challenged to institute prosecution at once. He also discussed with me the general terms of the report, and the fact that the matters which appeared to be most serious had occurred before the war period, before the establishment of controls.
I have had some experience in the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. I was connected with one case the Minister of Justice did not cite. That was the case against the coal industry, Rex v. Canadian Import Company. I conducted that prosecution for Mr. McGregor, and from my own experience in that case I can testify that I was the one who determined the evidence to be brought before the court, and that there was no attempt by Mr. McGregor or anyone else to direct me in the kind of case I should make before the court.
I was of opinion that unless there was a continuation of the facts which were more than two years old, section 1141 of the code would apply. I think that section is worthy of being quoted:
No action, suit or information shall be brought or laid for any penalty or forfeiture under any act, except within two years after the cause of action arises or after the offence for which such penalty or forfeiture is imposed is committed, unless the time is otherwise limited by any act or by-law.
The time for prosecution under section 498 of the Criminal Code or under the Combines Investigation Act is not limited. In the case of corporations it is a prosecution for a penalty, because both the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act provide that in the case of a corporation there is nothing but a penalty.
This matter arose and was discussed in the coal cases. There it was proved that the series of facts upon which we relied had
Combines Investigation Act commenced more than two years before the prosecution, but had continued right up to the time of the prosecution. The objection was urged, nevertheless, that the prosecutions were outlawed, but that objection was dismissed on the ground stated in the headnote:
It having been established that there was continuity in the acts charged of combining together with a view to unduly restricting the coal industry by lessening competition and fixing a common price, section 1141 of the Criminal Code does not apply to bar the action in question.
That is the headnote to the judgment of the Quebec court of appeals in the case of Rex v. Canadian Import Company and others, reported at 62 Canadian Criminal Cases, page 342. That followed a decision of the Ontario court of appeals in the case of Rex v. Elliott, reported at 9 Canadian Criminal Cases, page 505. Since 1906 it has become article 1141. Lawyers know this provision. It goes back to the time when the united Canada's statute was passed by the parliament of that province. The preamble stated that it was desirable to grant immunity to His Majesty's subjects being brought before the court to face allegations of long-past offences. It was stated that there should be a general limitation, which was enacted at that time and which has been continued. As I say, in 1906 it was article 930 of the Criminal Code but is now article 1141.
Even if code section 930, which limits certain proceedings to two years after the offence could be held to apply to a prosecution by indictment,_
. That is a prosecution of an individual by indictment where the individual was susceptible to punishment by imprisonment. Even if it could be held to apply to that,
-it did not apply to bar this prosecution for the offence was a continuing one.
The reason for the dismissal of this objection, and which was urged against me in the coal prosecution, was the continuity of the acts establishing the conspiracy. It was my view that the controls during the war period had put an end to what had gone on before, and that prices from that time onwards had been under the control of the flour controller, acting for the wartime prices and trade board.
I had this advantage over the Minister of Justice, that I had some knowledge of what had taken place during the period when Canadian industries were under control. It was my opinion that, if the controllers had been satisfied at the time that their directions were being carried out during that period when, for the security of this country and for the security of this parliament we had to have the co-operation of Canadian industries, it would not be proper for us to say that what they had done under the impression that they were serving this Canadian nation in

Supply
a patriotic fashion should afterward be made the subject of prosecution before the courts after the war was over.
For that reason, I concurred in this view that we should not attempt to prosecute for things that were more than two years old if we were not prepared to prosecute for what had happened during the period when those industries were under the constant direction of our controllers. Unless there were facts that were subsequent to the existence of the controls, it would not be in the public interest to have the prosecutions instituted. There were a whole series of things which interfered with the ordinary administration of the Combines Investigation Act. I was not convinced that the judgment in the dental supplies case should be pressed as far as Mr. McGregor felt it could be extended. Nevertheless, it was there and it said, in effect, that when dealing with corporations you had to prove not only that the officials of the corporation had those documents in their possession, but that the documents had been authorized by the board of directors or by someone in authority.
We were not in a position to make that proof or to meet the challenge, if the report had been published, that prosecutions be instituted. I felt that the officers and directors of those companies were entitled to the opinion that, during the period of control when they were carrying out the instructions of the controllers, they were acting in a manner that would not get them into trouble. And I now feel it is only fair to the Minister of Justice that I should inform the house that he had discussed these matters with me, and I had concurred in the line of conduct he was adopting. I should bear, therefore, a portion of the responsibility, if there is responsibility, for attempting to carry out the implied or expressed undertaking given to Canadian industry that if they did their best to help us win the war, they were not going to be pilloried afterwards under the Combines Investigation Act.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
It
is plain now to all of us, Mr. Speaker, after reading this bill, that the government is not going to pay an increased compensation for all reactors but is simply going to pay beef price for reactors which go to the tank. The other night I said something about statements

that had been made inside and outside the house with regard to the fact that the government was intending to pay an increased compensation for reactors. I should like to quote from page 2737 of Hansard of April 29, 1949, where that question was asked by Mr. Daniel of Oxford. I quote the question in order that the answer given by the parliamentary assistant (Mr. McCubbin) will be plain. It is as follows:
I should like to address a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), as reported on page 2239 of Hansard, concerning increases in the compensation paid farmers who have lost cattle under the area T.B. tests, is the minister's parliamentary assistant prepared to say that these payments will be made this year?
Here is the answer of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin):
I should like to thank the member for giving me notice of his question. In reply may I say that it might not be possible to reach some of the things we should like to reach before the end of this session, but I can assure the member that it is the intention of the government to increase the compensation paid to T.B. reactors, and also to make it retroactive. If it is not done before the end of this session, it will be one of the first things done by this government after the election.
If it was not the intention of the government to pay increased compensation for all reactors, the impression was most certainly left with delegations coming to Ottawa, with people outside the house, and with members within the house that this was to be done.
For a moment or two, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something about reactors. In the true sense of the word all cattle that react to the tuberculin tests for T.B. are reactors. In the quotation I just read from Hansard it was quite plain that the compensation was to be increased for T.B. reactors. That is the parliamentary assistant's statement. Now the government come along and say that, by the fact that they pay an increased compensation for reactors which go to the tank, they are doing what they said they would do and are fulfilling the promises made to delegations and to people across the country. I think that is a narrow margin on which the government are basing the facts.
As reported at page 2239 of Hansard of April 1, 1949, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made this statement:

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
A final decision has not been made and for that reason I am not able to say exactly what it will be. I am able to state that those who are concerned with the matter have been in to see us and they did not ask for any more than we were considering giving, so I think it likely there will be satisfaction when an announcement is finally made.
Animal Contagious Diseases Act
I would direct attention to the words "they did not ask for any more than we were considering giving." They may have considered it, but they are certainly not doing it.
As I said on Friday night, the compensation paid back in 1903 was identical with the compensation which is being paid today. Does it sound reasonable to you, Mr. Speaker, or to any other hon. member of this House of Commons, that the compensation to be paid in 1949 should be the same as that which was paid in 1903? In 1918 it was thought advisable to increase the compensation by a considerable amount; and as I stated on Friday, the compensation was increased to $80 for grade cattle and to $250 for purebred cattle. That would mean that, if paid on the two-thirds basis, the farmers at that time would receive $53.33 for grades and $166.66 for purebreds. On September 23 the Minister of Agriculture, as reported at page 223 of Hansard, made this statement:
Mr. Chairman, the answer today is the same as it was a year ago. About ten per cent of the cattle that are reactors go into the tank. The increased price of cattle does not hurt the man who is being paid compensation unless there is a large proportion of the animal infected because it is only then that it goes into the tank. If an animal is worth $200 this year and it was worth only $50 ten years ago, the compensation is on the same basis, but the remainder of the animal is sold and the individual gets the return. If his return is based on the $200 price he may get the greater part of the $200 and he gets the compensation as well.
Then here is the particular sentence I wish to stress:
It is not correct to say that because the price had gone up on cattle the compensation ought to go up. The compensation is not the whole thing.
The compensation is not the whole thing, Mr. Speaker, but the compensation is the greater part of the thing for those people who lose cattle in the T.B. test. As I said on Friday night, nobody that I know of- and I have asked various people who should know-has kicked about the amount of money received for reactors that went to the tank. The farmers were satisfied to take their losses on those tankers. What they are kicking about is the amount of money they get for reactors that do not go to the tank; and there are a great many more of those than there are those which are tankers. The delegations asked for an increase in the compensation for all reactors, not just those which went to the tanks.
In that same statement the Minister of Agriculture said that he brought in this bill last year. I think probably he erred slightly there, because I do not remember its coming in last year. I have checked up the records and cannot find any place where it was brought in.

Animal Contagious Diseases Act

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. I was mistaken in saying it was brought in last year. It was drafted but not brought in.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
I reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that what the people across the country expected, in view of the speeches made previous to the election, was that an increase would be made in the compensation paid for all reactors. I reiterate that statement. After taking a considerable beating in the 1940's, in view of the fact that cattle prices had increased considerably-I will say that they are probably three times what they were in 1903-it is not fair to expect people to accept now the same compensation that they accepted in 1903. I say that especially in view of the fact that the government of the day in 1918 thought it advisable to increase the compensation. If there was reason in 1918 to increase the compensation there is a far greater reason today to increase the compensation for T.B. reactors. I again ask the government and the Minister of Agriculture to reconsider the matter and increase the compensation to the value placed on the animal in the act, and not to take it down to two-thirds of the value. That would simply mean changing the figures in the act. That was what happened in 1922. The government of that day tried to reduce it from $250 to $150. There was such a strong case put up in the House of Commons that the figure was reduced only to $200.
I repeat that if there was just reason in 1918 to increase it, there is certainly a far greater reason to increase the compensation today. I hope the government will see fit to change their opinion and make the value as it is in the act today, namely, the total value, the compensation value without the two-thirds being taken off.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to say a word on this matter on second reading. This afternoon the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) mentioned national cheese week. If we are to have cheese to export to pay for other products that we wish to import we shall have to give some consideration to the men who produce it. Now is a good time and this is a good place for the government to exhibit that interest in the production of food and wealth which means so much to this country.
On Friday last I mentioned unemployment insurance, and similar things which were designed to tide people over difficult times. We are in perfect accord with unemployment insurance and with the assistance given to veterans. I could also mention the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. When they have difficult times and dried-out years in the west, Ontario farmers and others do not object to 
nor protest against the payments which are made to farmers in lieu of crops. When expropriation proceedings are taken the parties interested do not expect the arbitration boards to pay as little as they can get away with. They expect the arbitration boards to award a fair price for whatever real estate or property is expropriated. I could also mention the national health program. As far as national health is concerned, I think a lot more could be done to improve the nutritional value of certain foods that may be produced.
For a moment or two I am going to refer to some of the things that were said in days gone by by other people in dealing with this same measure. On April 16, 1918, the Hon. Mr. Crerar then minister of agriculture had this to say as reported at page 801 of Hansard:
I think a word of explanation will suffice for this resolution. At the time this act was originally passed the values upon which compensation was based for the slaughter of condemned animals were fixed by statute, in the case of cattle $60 per head and for pigs and sheep $15 per head, and the compensation allowed when animals were condemned and slaughtered was two-thirds of the value set by statute. Owing to the increased value of these animals at the present time, the compensation allowed when they are ordered to be destroyed does not adequately compensate their owners. The intention of the act when originally drafted, as I understand it, was to encourage the reporting to the proper authorities of animals which might be affected by some contagious disease, so that they could be properly examined, and if found a menace, destroyed. I think it is only proper that now, when the value of these animals has increased, and in some cases doubled, beyond what it was at the time the act was originally passed, the limit upon which compensation can be fixed should be raised, and that is the purpose of the resolution.
Conditions in April, 1918, and today are comparable. All I can say with respect to the action of the government is that it is similar to many other actions taken during the war and after. I could sum it up in five words, "Too little and too late."
On April 20, 1923, the Hon. Mr. Motherwell, also speaking in this house as minister of agriculture, said, as reported at page 2047 of Hansard:
This is the usual resolution which precedes a money bill and while it was discussed incidentally a few weeks ago I think it is well to go into it further at this time. The main feature of the resolution proposes to reduce the indemnity for slaughtered animals, that is purebreds, from $200 for each head to $150. Our reason for doing that is to conform to the general reduction of values in live stock, both commercial and purebred.
The government of that day was quite prone to reduce compensation when the prices of animals were down, but they are very hesitant today about bringing them up when prices are high. As I said on Friday last, the farmers are going to be bitterly disappointed. I hold in my hand a copy of a

presentation which was made to the government earlier this year. I intend to quote two or three paragraphs from it.
